Title: go-webthings
Summary: Guides for building a website with go-webthings. You bring the templates and choose the modules; go-webthings runs the database, the admin, pages, media, languages and the modules.

Guides.Title: Introduction
Guides.Summary: go-webthings is a Go library that runs the backend of a website: the database, the admin, accounts and permissions, pages, media, languages, themes and modules. You bring the templates and choose the modules.
Guides.Body:
What it is

Your website is a small Go program. Its main.go creates an app with a configuration, adds the modules it wants and starts serving. go-webthings does the rest: it creates the database tables, runs the admin at /admin/ (or a path of your own) and renders the public site with your templates.

app := webthings.New(webthings.Config{
    Name:      "My site",
    Locales:   locales.Config{Default: "en", Enabled: []string{"en", "nl"}},
    Templates: os.DirFS("templates"),
})

err := app.Use(
    publishing.Module("news", "News"),
    events.Module("agenda", "Agenda"),
)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

if err := app.ListenAndServe(ctx, ":8080"); err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

The result is a single binary. It runs on SQLite without any other service, or on PostgreSQL or MySQL.

What it is not

  • It is not a hosted service or an application to install. You build your own site with it, usually from the starter repository; see Getting started.
  • It has no design of its own. The public site is your templates; the starter's default theme is plain HTML to build on, next to a finished one, editorial.
  • It is not a headless CMS: pages are rendered on the server with Go templates, or with another engine through a renderer. Config.API adds a read-only JSON API of the published content, for apps; see Content API.
  • It is not an HTML editor. Editors write formatted text, which is stored as Markdown; raw HTML in that text is left out, never rendered.

What the site brings

Part Where What it is
Configuration main.go webthings.Config: name, database, languages, mail, storage; see Configuration
Modules main.go the app.Use(...) list, one entry per instance such as news or agenda
Templates templates/<theme>/ the layout, page, 404 and search templates, and a folder per module
Assets templates/<theme>/assets/ CSS, JavaScript and images, served at /theme/
Translations translations/ the site's own texts per language, in .po files

A site can also add its own Go code: template functions, a seed for an empty database, or a module of its own.

What go-webthings runs

  • The database and its tables, created and updated at start.
  • The admin, with sign-in, password reset, accounts and groups.
  • The page tree, the routes in every language, and scheduled publishing.
  • The media library, with resized copies of images, made after the upload or on their first request.
  • Site settings, themes, sitemap.xml, robots.txt and the site search.
  • E-mail for the modules, through the sender you configure.
  • Every module's admin section, public pages, Atom and RSS feeds, template functions and components.

The main parts

  • Pages form the page tree. Every page has a title, slug, description and Markdown text per language. A page can also carry a module instance, which then serves everything below it. See Pages.
  • Media is the library of images and files that pages and modules use. See Media and images.
  • Site settings hold the title and tagline per language, the languages, the timezone, the logo, contact details and social media profiles. The layout template gets them; see Templates and Languages.
  • Themes are the folders in templates/. Editors pick the active one in the admin. See Themes.
  • Accounts and groups decide who may do what. Administrators may do everything; editors get the rights of their groups. See Accounts and permissions.
  • The admin at /admin/ has a section for each of these and for every module instance. See Editing and publishing.
  • The frontend turns a request into a page: it finds the page, builds the data and renders your templates. See Templates.
  • Modules add content and features, such as news, an agenda, comments or a newsletter. Each instance has a key and its own admin section. See Using modules.
  • Components are parts of a page that modules offer to every template, such as {{commentThread "comments" .ID}} or {{newsletterForm "newsletter"}}. Core offers one as well, {{shareBar "" .Title}}. They come with plain default markup that a theme can replace.

How a request is served

Every request passes one router. Around it runs what every request gets: the visitor's address, a request ID, the security headers, the metrics, the access log when Config.AccessLog is set, and the recovery from panics, which answers 500 and keeps the site running. The metrics and the access log leave out the health and metrics addresses; see Deployment.

go-webthings' own addresses are routes of that router, and app.CorePaths() lists them (see routes in webthings.go). The admin's address is Config.AdminPath, /admin by default; the others are fixed:

/admin/          the admin, at Config.AdminPath
/media/          uploaded files and resized images
/theme/          the themes' assets
/assets/         Config.Assets or Config.ImportMap, when set
/_/              visitors' form posts to modules, core's stylesheets such as webthings.css, and the CSP reports
/sitemap.xml     every published page in every language
/robots.txt      allows every crawler and points to the sitemap
/healthz         answers 200 while the process runs
/readyz          answers 200 when the site can serve, 503 otherwise
/metrics         the metrics, only with Config.MetricsToken
/api/v1/         the content API, only with Config.API

A plain 404, not the site's 404 page, answers an address below /_/ that is no module's action, an address below /assets/ without Config.Assets or Config.ImportMap, and /metrics without Config.MetricsToken.

A module's form posts go to /_/<key>/, its visitor actions, past the protection against posts from other sites and a limit on the size of the post; see Visitor forms. The forms of bundled modules such as comments and the newsletter send a visitor whose post has mistakes back to the form, which shows the values again with a message at each field to correct; see A post with mistakes.

Once the app has started, every answer carries the security headers X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin: the answers of these routes and of the public site, the router's own redirects, and also /healthz, /readyz and /metrics. Pages, the 404 page and the answers of visitor actions also say which sites may show them in a frame, as Site settings › Security decides, a card only administrators can change; admin pages never may. See Deployment.

Every other request goes to the public site, through the middleware of modules such as redirects and stats, and then the output cache, which sends visitors a page it keeps in memory without rendering it again (see Deployment). Pages live in the database and can move, so the site finds the page itself:

  1. / redirects to the default language, for example /en/.
  2. The first path segment must be an enabled language. Anything else gets the 404 page.
  3. The rest of the path is looked up in that language's published page tree. Addresses are canonical: /en becomes /en/, and a trailing slash elsewhere is removed.
  4. A page without a module is rendered with page.gohtml inside layout.gohtml. It answers GET and HEAD; another method gets 405.
  5. A page with a module is served by that module's own router, at the page's address. Its routes are relative to the page, so the module works wherever editors place it, and its handlers see the whole path. A path or method it has no route for gets the 404 page.
  6. Nothing found renders 404.gohtml.

Before the app has started, only /healthz, /readyz and /metrics answer as usual; every other address gets 503.

With the news module on the page /news:

/en/                  the home page
/en/about/team        the page "team" below "about"
/en/news              the news module's route "/{$}": its list
/en/news/opening      the news module's route "/{slug}": a post
/en/news/feed.atom    the news module's Atom feed; feed.rss is the same in RSS
/en/search?q=clay     the search screen, unless a page has the path /search

Rendering uses the theme that is active in the site settings. Templates and assets that a theme lacks come from templates/default/.

Built on

go-webthings uses a few libraries by the same author:

  • go-router is the router every request passes, with named routes, and brings the middleware around it: the visitor's address, request IDs, security headers, compression, ETags, the output cache, throttles and the recovery from panics.
  • go-partial renders templates inside a layout, and only the content for HTMX requests.
  • go-form builds the admin's forms and the fields of visitors' forms from Go structs, reads and validates their posts, and brings the spam trap of visitors' forms. Posts from other websites are refused by Go's own cross-origin protection.
  • go-importmap serves the admin's files, the themes' assets, Config.Assets and Config.ImportMap with versioned addresses. The admin's htmx is vendored with it and checked at start.
  • go-translator reads the .po catalogues for the admin and for your templates' {{tl localizer "..."}} texts.
  • go-clue gives editors completion and checks in Go templates. The @dot line at the top of a generated template names its data type for it, and an @model line names the page or its content in any template, partials included (see Templates).

The main other dependencies are the three database drivers, sqlx, goldmark for Markdown and gen2brain/webp for WebP images. None of them needs cgo. The admin's text editor is built on ProseMirror, which comes with the admin as one JavaScript file, so it needs no build step and no CDN.

Next steps

  • Getting started runs the starter site.
  • Configuration lists every setting.
  • Pages and Templates explain how the site is built.
  • Using modules shows how to add and place modules.

Guides.Title: Getting started
Guides.Summary: Start a site from the starter repository, run it locally, and find your way around the admin and the templates.
Guides.Body:
What you need

  • Go 1.27 or newer.
  • Task to run the starter's commands. Each task is a single go command (go run, go generate, go build or go test), so plain go works too.
  • Nothing else: no C compiler, and no database server. The site uses SQLite in a folder of its own until you configure PostgreSQL or MySQL.

Copy the starter

The starter is a complete website: main.go with the configuration and the modules, and a templates/ folder with two themes. default/ is plain HTML without JavaScript that uses every field of its data; editorial/ is a finished design with HTMX navigation. Editors choose one under Theme in the admin.

git clone https://github.com/donseba/go-webthings-clone my-site
cd my-site

Change the module path in go.mod to your own. Until go-webthings has a tagged release, the starter's go.mod builds against a checkout next to it, so clone that too:

git clone https://github.com/donseba/go-webthings ../go-webthings

For now go-webthings itself builds only against development branches of go-partial, go-router, go-form, go-importmap and go-translator, in a Go workspace; its README names them. Run the starter in that workspace too.

The folder holds:

main.go         configuration and the list of modules
templates/      one folder per theme
  default/        the plain theme: layout, pages and one folder per module
  default/assets/ CSS, JavaScript and images, served at /theme/
  editorial/      a second, complete theme with HTMX navigation
importmap.json  the themes' JavaScript packages, vendored in assets/vendor/
translations/   the website's own texts per language (en.po, nl.po, ...)
var/            database and uploads, created on first start

Run it

task run

Open http://127.0.0.1:8092/ for the site and http://127.0.0.1:8092/admin/ for the admin. /admin is the default admin path; Config.AdminPath can move it. The starter's admin is in Dutch; this guide uses its English names, which WEBTHINGS_ADMIN_LANGUAGE=en task run shows.

The first start creates the database in var/, a published home page, and an administrator from WEBTHINGS_ADMIN_EMAIL and WEBTHINGS_ADMIN_PASSWORD. task run sets local defaults for both, admin@example.test and change-me-please; use your own for a real site. Once any account exists, these variables are ignored. Started without them, for example with WEBTHINGS_INSECURE_HTTP=true go run ., the site logs a one-time link, http://127.0.0.1:8092/admin/setup?token=…, where you create the first administrator yourself.

Lost the setup link? Open /admin/login: while no account exists, the sign-in page logs the link again, at level WARN and at most once a minute. Search the log for "no account exists yet". Or let the starter create an administrator:

go run . admin you@example.com

It prints a link, valid for one hour, where the account's owner chooses the password, so no password goes into the environment. The command also adds an administrator to a site that has accounts; an address that has an account is refused. It uses App.InviteAdministrator; see Accounts and permissions.

task run also sets WEBTHINGS_INSECURE_HTTP=true, so the admin's session cookie works over plain HTTP. Never set it in production.

While you work on the templates

task run serves the site as in production: templates are read once, and visitors get pages from the output cache. While you change the templates, run this instead:

task dev

It serves on the same address with WEBTHINGS_DEVELOPMENT=true, which sets Config.Development and Config.ReloadTemplates. Templates are read again from templates/ on every request, so an edit shows on the next request without a restart. A failing page shows the error with its template and line. A template with a problem, such as a function the site does not have, stops the start with all such problems listed (see Checking the templates at start). The output cache is off. The site logs development mode (WEBTHINGS_DEVELOPMENT): … when it starts. Never set it in production, because visitors would see the details of errors. Without it, a broken template gives visitors the theme's 500.gohtml in their language, without the error, which goes to the log; see Development mode.

Set up the site

After you create the first administrator with the setup link, the admin opens Getting started, in Dutch Aan de slag: a guide through what a new site needs. Its steps:

  1. Site: the languages, the timezone, and the site's title and tagline in each language.
  2. Theme: the theme, its colours and settings, and the logo.
  3. E-mail: how the site sends e-mail, and a test e-mail to you; see Deployment.
  4. Pages: a published page for each module and drafts of About us, Contact and Privacy; see Pages from the setup guide.
  5. Security: the Security card of Site settings, with the Content-Security-Policy; see Security settings.
  6. Finish: what is done and what was skipped, with next steps.

The Site, Theme and Security steps show the cards of Site settings and Theme, and every step saves at once. Skip for now leaves a step for later. The guide remembers which steps are done or skipped, also after a restart, and opens again at the first open step. Until you finish it, the dashboard shows "Finish setting up your site" with the steps done, such as "2 of 5 steps done", and Site settings links to it with Continue setup. Once it is finished, Open the setup guide on Site settings brings it back. Only administrators see the guide; editors never do.

Look around the admin

Sign in at /admin/. The navigation has a section for every part of the site:

  • Pages is the page tree. Every page has a title and a Web address per language, the last part of its address, made from the title when left empty; a page can show its own text or a module.
  • Media is the library of images and files that pages and modules use.
  • Site settings hold the site's title and tagline per language, the languages, the timezone, the logo and contact details, and the social media profiles. Theme chooses the design and its settings.
  • Accounts and Groups decide who may edit what.
  • Every module instance in main.go has a section of its own, such as News or Agenda.

To put a module on the site, create a page, choose the instance under Shows on this page and publish the page. The module then serves its list and detail pages below that page's address.

Change the modules

The modules are listed in siteModules in main.go, which main passes to app.Use and main_test.go starts too:

func siteModules() []webthings.Module {
    return []webthings.Module{
        publishing.Module("news", "News").Group("Content"),
        publishing.Module("blog", "Blog").Group("Content"),
        events.Module("agenda", "Agenda").Group("Agenda"),
        // …
    }
}

The first argument is the instance key, the second the title editors see. Group places the instance's admin section under a heading of the admin navigation. Add, remove or rename instances and restart. See Using modules, and https://modules.gowebthings.com for what each module offers.

Change the design

Everything visitors see comes from the active theme. This section describes templates/default/, the theme a new site starts with: plain HTML that uses every field of its data, without JavaScript; build your design around it and style it in templates/default/assets/site.css. templates/editorial/ has the same pages with a finished design, regions and fragments for HTMX, and its own settings; the starter's README describes it, and Themes covers themes.

  • layout.gohtml wraps every page and gets the site, the menu and the languages.
  • The layout places the tags of the page in <head> with {{slot "head"}}: WebThings writes the title, the description, the canonical and alternate links, the sharing tags, the icons, the feed links and the structured data. A regions/head.gohtml of your own adds tags to them (see Themes).
  • page.gohtml shows a page, 404.gohtml the "not found" page, and 500.gohtml the page visitors get when a template or a module fails, on its own without the layout (see 500.gohtml).
  • The layout loads its stylesheets with {{styles "webthings.css" "site.css"}}, which links go-partial's partial-errors.css, then these files, then the theme's values stylesheet, each with the file's Subresource Integrity (see Themes); {{assetScript "site.js" "type" "module"}} does the same for a script in assets/.
  • Module templates live in a folder named after the instance key, such as news/list.gohtml and news/post.gohtml.

After adding a module, write starting points for its templates:

task templates -- agenda

task templates -- site writes the layout with its head region and its stylesheet assets/site.css, and the page, 404 and search templates. Existing files are never overwritten, and a template that is still missing is reported in the log when the site starts, with the task templates -- <key> that writes it. The start also checks every template of every theme, and logs each problem as template problem with the file and the line; with task dev the site does not start until they are fixed (see Checking the templates at start). Templates explains which template gets which data, and Theme checklist lists what a theme needs.

Build it

task build

writes a single static binary to bin/website. It needs the templates/ and translations/ folders in the folder it runs in, and a writable state folder for the database and uploads (var/, or WEBTHINGS_STATE_DIR). Deployment covers running it in production, and Databases switching to PostgreSQL or MySQL. The site can also send a strict Content-Security-Policy, which administrators turn on under Site settings › Security (see A Content-Security-Policy of the site's own).

Next steps

  • Configuration lists every setting of webthings.Config.
  • Pages explains the page tree and how modules are placed on it.
  • Templates and Themes cover the design.
  • Languages covers multilingual sites and translating your template texts.

Guides.Title: Configuration
Guides.Summary: A site configures go-webthings with one Config value in its main.go. This guide lists every field, the starter's environment variables and the methods of the app.
Guides.Body:
An example

app := webthings.New(webthings.Config{
    Name:           "Atelier",
    StateDir:       "/var/lib/atelier",
    Driver:         "pgx",
    DSN:            os.Getenv("WEBTHINGS_DB_DSN"),
    Locales:        locales.Config{Default: "nl", Enabled: []string{"nl", "en"}},
    AdminLanguage:  "nl",
    AdminEmail:     os.Getenv("WEBTHINGS_ADMIN_EMAIL"),
    AdminPassword:  os.Getenv("WEBTHINGS_ADMIN_PASSWORD"),
    Templates:      os.DirFS("templates"),
    Translations:   translations,
    BaseURL:        "https://atelier.example",
    TrustedProxies: []string{"127.0.0.1"},
    Mail: mail.SMTP{
        Host:     "smtp.example.com",
        Username: os.Getenv("SMTP_USER"),
        Password: os.Getenv("SMTP_PASSWORD"),
        From:     "Atelier <hello@atelier.example>",
    },
})

Every field is optional. The fields are defined in webthings.go.

All fields

Field Default What it does
Name WebThings The admin's title, and the site title in every language on first start
StateDir var Folder for the SQLite database, uploads and catalogues that change the admin's texts
Driver sqlite Database driver: sqlite (sqlite3 works too), pgx or mysql
DSN SQLite file in StateDir How to reach the database
Locales English only Content languages on first start
AdminLanguage English Language of the admin, such as en or nl
AdminPath /admin Where the admin is served, such as /toolbox
AdminEmail, AdminPassword none The first administrator, on an empty database
Insecure false Allows the admin's session cookie over plain HTTP
Authorize built-in rules Replaces the admin's permission rules
Templates none The public site's templates, one folder per theme
Translations none: texts as written The site's own translations, from frontend.Translations
Funcs none Extra template functions
Renderer none Another template engine instead of Templates
ReloadTemplates false Reads the templates again for every request, for development
Assets none Files served at /assets/, with versioned addresses and go-partial's browser clients
ImportMap none An import map whose files are served at /assets/, with versioned addresses and go-partial's browser clients
FormTheme webthings The go-form theme that visitor forms in templates render with
BaseURL address of each request The public address, for absolute links
TrustedProxies none Reverse proxies whose forwarding headers are believed
Mail log only Sends e-mail from the modules and the admin
Storage StateDir/media Keeps uploaded media
CacheTTL 30 seconds How long settings and routes are kept in memory
OutputCacheTTL the site setting, 1 minute How long pages for visitors are kept in memory; overrides the site setting
ScheduleInterval 30 seconds How often scheduled publishing runs
Development false Shows failing templates in detail and stops the start for every template problem, for development
LogFormat none: the site's own logger text or json: logs to standard error, with request IDs
LogLevel Info The lowest level logged with LogFormat
AccessLog false Logs a line for every request
MetricsToken none: no /metrics Serves the metrics at /metrics to requests with this token
Telemetry none Tracing and other instrumentation
ContentSecurityPolicy the site setting, off The Content-Security-Policy: off, report-only or enforce; overrides the site setting
ContentSecuritySources none Sources the policy allows besides the site's own, by directive
API off The content API: the published content as JSON at /api/v1/

Site and admin

Name is the admin's title. On first start it also becomes the site title in every language; after that, editors change the title under Site settings.

AdminLanguage sets the language of the admin. English (en, the default) and Dutch (nl) are built in; see Languages. Modules also use it for e-mail to staff, such as a notification about a new form entry.

Authorize replaces the built-in rules, in which administrators may do everything and editors what their groups allow; without it, those rules apply. When set, it decides every check, also for administrators. It is asked about the Accounts and Groups screens too, so it can keep them from administrators, but it never opens them to editors. It must be safe for concurrent use: requests and work in the background ask it at the same time.

Authorize: func(ctx context.Context, user auth.User, permission admin.Permission) bool {
    // Editors may look at everything but change nothing.
    return user.IsAdmin() || permission.Action == admin.View
},

permission.Section is pages, media, site, accounts, groups or a module's key; permission.Action is one of read, create, edit, publish, delete, review and export. See Accounts and permissions.

Admin path

AdminPath is where the admin is served: /admin by default, or a path of your own, such as /toolbox.

AdminPath: "/toolbox",

The path starts with a slash and does not end with one. It has letters, digits, -, ., _ and ~ only, in one segment or more, such as /staff/admin, and no segment . or ... It cannot be one of the app's other addresses, or above or below one, such as /media, /_, /healthz or /assets/admin. Its first segment cannot be the code of an enabled language, such as /en or /en/admin: the admin would take that language's pages. Otherwise Start stops with an error. Later, the site settings refuse to enable a language with that code; see Languages.

Every address of the admin is below the path: the sign-in page at /toolbox/login, the setup link at /toolbox/setup?token=…, the event stream at /toolbox/presence and a module's section at /toolbox/<key>. The bare path leads to the dashboard. Nothing else depends on the path: the admin, core and the modules link to admin pages by route name. Go code builds those links with app.AdminURL or, in a module, env.AdminURL. app.AdminPath() returns the path, for tests and tools.

robots.txt does not name the admin, so a path of your own is not published there. Admin pages answer with X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow instead, which keeps them out of search results also when other sites link to them. The session cookie, wt_admin, is set for the whole site, so editors get their edit links on public pages. The cookie that carries the admin's messages across a redirect, wt_admin_flash, is set for the admin's path only.

First start only

Some fields only fill an empty database:

  • Locales sets the content languages and the default language, for example locales.Config{Default: "nl", Enabled: []string{"nl", "en"}}. The default must be one of the enabled languages. Later changes are made in the admin under Site settings; see Languages.
  • AdminEmail and AdminPassword create the first administrator while there are no accounts at all. The password needs at least 12 characters, or the start fails. Once any account exists, both are ignored. Without them, the start logs a one-time link below the admin path, such as /admin/setup?token=…, where you create the first administrator. Without that token, and once any account exists, the address answers 404. See Accounts and permissions.
  • Name becomes the site title in every language, as above.

The first start also creates and publishes a home page, and sets the timezone to UTC.

Database and files

StateDir is created at start if it does not exist. It holds site.sqlite when the site uses SQLite without a DSN and media/ when Storage is not set. A translations/ folder there, when you add one, holds catalogues that change the admin's texts; the admin reads it and never writes to it. See Languages.

Driver and DSN choose the database. An empty DSN with sqlite or sqlite3 uses StateDir/site.sqlite. See Databases for PostgreSQL and MySQL.

Storage keeps uploaded files somewhere else than StateDir/media, for example an S3 bucket. It is a media.Storage. Without it, the app keeps them with media.NewFilesystem in StateDir/media and serves them itself at /media/; see Media and images.

Templates

Templates is a file system with one folder per theme, such as templates/default/, or a single theme with layout.gohtml at its root. Without Templates or Renderer, every page shows a short text that asks for templates.

Templates: os.DirFS("templates"),

Translations are the site's own translations of the templates' texts, read from .po files with frontend.Translations. The starter loads them like this:

translations, err := frontend.Translations("translations")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

// in the Config:
Translations: translations,

Templates get tl, tn, ctl and ctn from them. Core translates its own texts with them too: the title of the 404 page, the heading and the message of the error page, the names of social networks, go-form's texts in visitor forms, and the names of months and days and the date patterns, which replace the built-in ones, also those of English and Dutch. Without Translations, every text shows as written. app.Frontend.SetTranslations does the same after Start, before the site serves. See Languages.

Funcs adds template functions to every template in Templates:

Funcs: []template.FuncMap{{
    "upper": strings.ToUpper,
}},

A site function with the same name as a module's function replaces it in every template, so give the site's functions names of their own unless you mean to replace one. A name go-partial uses, such as url, content, locale, localizer, slot, hasSlot, requiredSlot, deferredSlot, targetHeader, targetValue or targetIs, or any name starting with _, stops the start with render.ErrReserved; see Templates.

Renderer replaces Templates with another template engine; when both are set, Renderer is used. See Another template engine.

ReloadTemplates reads the templates again for every request, so edits show without a restart. It also turns the output cache off, unless OutputCacheTTL is set; see Production. Use it during development only; otherwise every template is read once.

Assets is an extra file system served at /assets/, like the files of an import map below. Start gives each file a version from its content. {{importmap_url "site.css"}} is the file's versioned address, such as /assets/site.css?v=9b2ca0fe143be1a4, which browsers may keep for a year; a plain /assets/site.css is checked with the file's ETag on every request. Core adds go-partial's browser clients among the files, so {{importmap}} maps partial-flash, partial-sse and partial-interactions, with their integrity; a file of that name in Assets replaces core's. With ReloadTemplates, a changed file gets a new version without a restart, and no file carries integrity, in the import map or in the tags of importmap_script and importmap_style, since it may change under a page. Folders are not listed. A theme's own files belong in its assets/ folder instead, served at /theme/; see Themes.

ImportMap is an import map of go-importmap, such as one of vendored packages loaded with importmap.FromFS. Its files are served at /assets/ with versioned addresses: a request for a file's current version may be kept for a year, any other is checked with the file's ETag. Templates get {{importmap}}, the import map for the layout's <head>, and {{importmap_url "file"}}, a file's versioned address; functions of the site's own with these names replace them. Core adds go-partial's browser clients to the map, partial-flash, partial-sse and partial-interactions, unless the map has such a name already; a client file among the map's own files is used instead, and core's copies are served at /assets/ too. The import map, and the tags of importmap_script and importmap_style, carry the integrity of every file, the clients' included, except for a map made with go-importmap's assets.Reload, whose files may change while the site runs; the files of importmap.FromFS keep it, also with ReloadTemplates. See HTMX. Set Assets or ImportMap, not both: with both, Start stops with an error.

FormTheme names the go-form theme that visitor forms in templates render with: {{form_field .Form "name" nil}} and go-form's other functions; see Visitor forms and Themes. Empty uses frontend.FormTheme, webthings: go-form's markup with the classes of webthings.css. A site with CSS of its own registers a theme with its classes, with go-form's templates package, before the site serves:

_, err := templates.RegisterClassTheme("atelier", templates.ThemeClasses{
    Wrapper:     templates.StyleOption{Class: "field"},
    Description: templates.StyleOption{Class: "help"},
    Error:       templates.StyleOption{Class: "error"},
    Honeypot:    templates.StyleOption{Class: templates.HoneypotClass},
})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

// in the Config:
FormTheme: "atelier",

Honeypot gives the spam trap a class, here form-honeypot, which webthings.css hides; a theme without webthings.css hides it in its own stylesheet. A theme without Honeypot gives the trap form-honeypot and an inline style that hides it. A Content-Security-Policy without 'unsafe-inline' blocks that style, so then only a stylesheet that hides form-honeypot keeps the trap out of sight (see Visitor forms).

app.Frontend.SetFormTheme(name) does the same after Start, before the site serves.

Production

BaseURL is the public address, such as https://example.com. It is used in sitemap.xml, robots.txt, share links, {{absURL}}, feeds and the IDs of their entries, and links in e-mail. Without it, each request's own address is used: its Host header and whether it came over TLS, or what a trusted proxy reports. The start then logs a warning, unless Insecure is set. The admin offers its password reset only with both BaseURL and Mail (or with Insecure), because a link made from the Host header could point to another site.

TrustedProxies lists the reverse proxies in front of the site, as IP addresses or CIDR ranges such as 127.0.0.1 or 10.0.0.0/8. Only requests from these addresses may name the visitor's address in X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP or Forwarded, and the site's address in X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Host, or else in the proto= and host= of Forwarded. Behind such a proxy, r.RemoteAddr holds the visitor's address with port 0, such as 198.51.100.7:0, so handlers that read it see the visitor too. An entry that is not an address or range stops the start with an error.

Insecure sends the admin's session cookie without the Secure flag, so signing in works over plain HTTP. It also offers the password reset without Mail and BaseURL, with the link written to the log. It is for local development only; never set it in production.

Mail sends the modules' e-mail, the admin's password reset links and the setup guide's test e-mail. mail.SMTP is built in; without a sender, messages are written to the log. A sender that implements mail.Describer says in the setup guide how it sends. See E-mail.

CacheTTL is how long site settings, theme values and the published routes are kept in memory. Changes made in the same process apply at once; changes made by another process on the same database show up within this time. Zero means 30 seconds and a negative value turns the cache off. The admin keeps what it found of the links to pages for this time at most too.

OutputCacheTTL overrides how long the output cache keeps pages for visitors in memory, so they are sent again without being rendered. The cache is on by default: editors set its time and memory under Site settings → Performance, 1 minute and 32 MB unless they change them. A positive OutputCacheTTL keeps pages that long, whatever the setting; a negative one turns the cache off. Zero follows the setting, except that Development and ReloadTemplates turn the cache off. When the configuration decides the time in one of these ways, Site settings → Performance shows the time that applies for The site keeps pages in memory for, or Off, disabled, with the note "Set by the server configuration."; saving the card keeps the stored time and saves its other fields. Changes made on this server show at once: in the admin, at planned publication, and from Go through the core services and the bundled modules. For other changes, such as data the site's pages show from elsewhere, call app.Changed() after the commit. Changes made by another server, and what changes with time alone, show within the cache's time. Deployment says what the cache keeps, such as a whole page and an HTMX navigation of the same address side by side, and when it renders a page again; Caching and testing a module says what modules do for it.

OutputCacheTTL: 5 * time.Minute,

ScheduleInterval is how often planned publications are carried out. Zero means 30 seconds; a negative value stops the background scheduler, for example in tests that call RunSchedules themselves.

ContentSecurityPolicy overrides the site setting Content-Security-Policy under Site settings → Security: off, report-only or enforce (site.CSPOff, site.CSPReportOnly, site.CSPEnforce). Empty follows the setting, which is off until an administrator changes it; any other value stops the start with an error. With a policy set, the card shows it, disabled, with the note "Set by the server configuration.", and saving the card keeps the stored setting. ContentSecuritySources adds sources to the policy by directive, besides the site's own, such as a host of fonts. They come on top of the setting's Outside sources and the theme's "csp" in theme.json. The start checks them with site.CheckCSPSources and stops with an error for a source it refuses, such as 'unsafe-inline' or *. See A Content-Security-Policy of the site's own.

ContentSecurityPolicy:  site.CSPEnforce,
ContentSecuritySources: map[string][]string{"font-src": {"https://fonts.example.com"}},

Deployment explains these settings in context.

The content API

API turns on the content API, which serves the published content as JSON at /api/v1/, for apps and other frontends; see Content API. It is an api.Config of package api:

API: api.Config{
    Enabled:        true,
    AllowedOrigins: []string{"https://app.example.com"},
},

Enabled serves the API; it is off by default. AllowedOrigins lists the sites whose pages may read the API in the browser (CORS): an origin such as https://app.example.com, * for every site or *.example.com for the subdomains of example.com. Without it, the API sends no CORS headers; with it, a request whose Origin is not allowed is answered with 403. RateLimit is how many requests one client, known by its address, may make per RateWindow: zero means 300, a negative value turns the limit off, and a zero RateWindow means a minute. More get 429 with Retry-After. Behind a reverse proxy, the limit needs TrustedProxies, as above.

While the API is on, /api/v1 is one of CorePaths(): no language can have the code api and no top-level page the slug api. Deployment says how it is cached and limited behind a proxy.

Logs, metrics and development

Development shows a failing template in detail, on the site and in the admin: the template and the line, with status 500. It also makes {{debug .}} show the value it gets. Use it on your own machine only. Without it, a failing template is logged and the visitor gets the theme's 500.gohtml with status 500, in the page's language, with the theme's partials and the page's View for @model. A theme without one gives go-partial's plain error page, with status 500, the heading "Internal Server Error" and the message "Something went wrong. Please try again.", both translated into the page's language with Translations, and that language in lang. It never names the failed template or the error. The admin shows an error page of its own, in the admin's language, or the message "The request failed. Please try again." for part of a page. {{debug .}} then shows nothing. A site's own Renderer is not affected. Development also turns the output cache off, unless OutputCacheTTL is set; responses then say in X-Cache how the cache answered: hit, miss or skip. See Deployment.

Start checks every template of every theme with the site's functions and logs each problem at WARN as template problem, with the file, the line and a hint. With Development it fails with all of them at once (ErrTemplates), and a template call that would show nothing, such as {{posts "nieuws" 3}} for an instance key the site does not have, an asset file the theme does not have or an unknown {{theme}} setting, fails its page. Without it, Start fails only when every page of the active theme would fail: its layout, regions or partials do not parse or call a function the site does not have, such as one of a module removed from app.Use; such calls are logged once at WARN as template mistake and show nothing. See Checking the templates at start.

LogFormat, text or json, makes the start log to standard error in that format and makes that logger slog's default. Any other value stops the start with an error. LogLevel is the lowest level logged, a slog.Level; the zero value is Info. Without LogFormat, go-webthings logs with slog.Default() as the site set it up, and LogLevel does nothing.

AccessLog logs a line for every request but those to the health and metrics addresses below, at level Info: method, path without the query, status, bytes, duration, route class and request ID. See Deployment.

Every request has an ID: the X-Request-ID header a proxy sent, when it has at most 64 letters, digits, -, _, . or :, or else a new one. Every response names it in X-Request-ID, also before Start, and webthings.RequestID(ctx) returns it. With LogFormat, every line logged with a request's context, such as slog.ErrorContext(r.Context(), …), carries it as request_id. A site with a logger of its own leaves LogFormat empty and wraps its handler with webthings.LogHandler:

handler := slog.NewJSONHandler(os.Stdout, nil)
slog.SetDefault(slog.New(webthings.LogHandler(handler)))

A panic in a handler, such as a module's, does not stop the site. The request gets a plain 500, and slog.Default() logs panic recovered at level Error, with the panic, method, path, request ID and stack. When the answer had already started, the connection is cut instead, so the visitor does not get half a page that looks complete. The access log, the metrics and Telemetry.Middleware still see the request, with its 500 or the status already sent. Before Start, a panic is recovered and logged with its request ID too.

Three addresses are answered before the site, its middleware and sessions, to GET and HEAD requests; other methods go on to the site, which answers with its 404 page. /healthz answers 200 while the process runs. /readyz answers 200 when the app can serve (see Ready below) and 503 otherwise. /metrics serves the metrics only when MetricsToken is set, to requests with Authorization: Bearer <token>; without a token it answers a plain 404. All three answers are sent with Cache-Control: no-store. A site can also serve Metrics() itself, for example on an address only its monitoring reaches. See Deployment.

Telemetry plugs in instrumentation such as tracing. Middleware wraps every request except those three, like the access log and the metrics. That includes the answers the router gives itself, such as the redirect of //en/ to /en/. RenderStages run in every render of the themes' and the admin's templates, and RenderEvents receive go-partial's diagnostic events. Core brings no tracing library; see Deployment.

Compression, how long browsers and caches keep pages, and the output cache's time and memory are not fields but site settings, under Site settings → Performance; only OutputCacheTTL can override one of them. See Deployment. Whether other sites may show the pages in a frame is a site setting too, under Site settings → Security, which only administrators can change. That card also holds the Content-Security-Policy, which ContentSecurityPolicy overrides, and its outside sources (see Production). The site sends the headers for them, and its other security headers, itself; see Deployment. How many items each Atom and RSS feed lists is a site setting as well, Items in feeds under Site settings → General: 10, 20, 50 or 100, 20 by default. In Go it is site.Settings.FeedSize; FeedLimit() gives the number in effect, site.DefaultFeedSize (20) for zero, and saving a number below zero or above site.MaxFeedSize (100) fails with site.ErrInvalid. See Search and SEO.

The starter's environment variables

The starter's main.go reads these variables. They are the starter's own choice: change them, or add more, in your copy.

Variable Sets Starter default
WEBTHINGS_NAME Name My website
WEBTHINGS_STATE_DIR StateDir var
WEBTHINGS_DB_DRIVER Driver sqlite
WEBTHINGS_DB_DSN DSN empty
WEBTHINGS_ADMIN_LANGUAGE AdminLanguage nl
WEBTHINGS_ADMIN_EMAIL AdminEmail empty; task run and task dev set a local default
WEBTHINGS_ADMIN_PASSWORD AdminPassword empty; task run and task dev set a local default
WEBTHINGS_INSECURE_HTTP Insecure, when true empty; task run and task dev set true
WEBTHINGS_DEVELOPMENT Development and ReloadTemplates, when true empty; task dev sets true
WEBTHINGS_BASE_URL BaseURL empty
WEBTHINGS_TRUSTED_PROXIES TrustedProxies, separated by commas empty
WEBTHINGS_CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY ContentSecurityPolicy empty: the site setting
WEBTHINGS_SMTP_HOST Mail: a mail.SMTP to this server empty: e-mail goes to the log
WEBTHINGS_SMTP_PORT its Port 587
WEBTHINGS_SMTP_USERNAME, WEBTHINGS_SMTP_PASSWORD its Username and Password empty
WEBTHINGS_SMTP_FROM its From none; required with WEBTHINGS_SMTP_HOST
WEBTHINGS_LISTEN the address to serve on 127.0.0.1:8092
WEBTHINGS_THEME the theme task templates writes into default

With WEBTHINGS_SMTP_HOST set, the starter stops at once when WEBTHINGS_SMTP_FROM is missing or WEBTHINGS_SMTP_PORT is not a number. It sets the languages in code (nl and en). Set WEBTHINGS_BASE_URL, WEBTHINGS_TRUSTED_PROXIES and the mail server before going live. With WEBTHINGS_DEVELOPMENT=true it logs development mode (WEBTHINGS_DEVELOPMENT): … at start; never set it in production. It reads no variables for logs or metrics; add them in your copy when you need them.

The starter also has an admin command: go run . admin you@example.com creates an administrator with InviteAdministrator (see below) and prints the link, valid for one hour, where its owner chooses the password. Without BaseURL, the link is on the address of WEBTHINGS_LISTEN.

The app

webthings.New(config) applies the defaults and returns an *App; it opens nothing yet. The app's methods:

Method What it does
Use(modules...) Adds module instances. Call it before Start. It fails on an invalid or duplicate key.
Start(ctx) Opens the database, applies the schemas, creates the first administrator (or logs the setup link), settings and home page, sets up the modules and the admin, and starts the background work: the scheduler, and a cleanup of expired sessions, sign-in attempts and reset links at start and then every hour.
ListenAndServe(ctx, addr) Listens on addr and calls Serve.
Serve(ctx, listener) Calls Start unless that already happened, then serves on listener until ctx is cancelled, and lets running requests finish. It closes the listener and the app when it returns. Use it with a listener of your own, such as one from systemd socket activation. The "serving" log line, and without BaseURL the setup link, show the address it really listens on, also with :0.
ServeHTTP(w, r) The app is an http.Handler. Before Start it answers 503, except at /healthz, /readyz (which reports not ready) and /metrics (a plain 404 without MetricsToken).
Close() Stops the background work, closes the modules (last added first), the storage and the database.
WriteTemplates(dir, key) Writes starting points for a module's templates, or for "site". Needs no Start. An unknown key gives an error that lists the keys it accepts.
TemplateKeys() The keys WriteTemplates accepts: "site", then the modules with templates in the order they were added. Needs no Start.
Translations(dir, args) The translations command: writes translations.pot, or checks the .po files. Needs no Start.
TranslationCatalog() Every text Translations writes, as go-translator's *extract.Catalog: the templates' texts, core's, the calendar names and the modules' form texts. Needs no Start.
RunSchedules(ctx) Carries out planned publications now and returns how many changed.
Changed() Tells the app that what visitors see changed, so the output cache renders its pages again. Call it after the commit of a change the app does not see itself, such as data the site's pages show from elsewhere. Writes through the core services and the bundled modules tell it themselves.
Service(key) The API of a started module instance, or nil.
AdminURL(name, args...) The address of a named admin route, such as AdminURL("admin.login") or AdminURL("admin.pages.edit", "id", id). Empty before Start. It panics on an unknown route or parameter.
AdminPath() Where the admin is served, such as /admin, for tests and tools; see Admin path. Links use AdminURL. Needs no Start.
CorePaths() The addresses the app serves itself, next to the site's pages: the admin at its path, /healthz, /readyz, /metrics, /_, /media, /assets, /theme, /sitemap.xml and /robots.txt, and /api/v1 while API turns the content API on, read from the app's own routes. Needs no Start.
IsCorePath(path) Whether path is one of CorePaths or below one: /theme/site.css is, /themes is not. Modules ask env.IsCorePath. Needs no Start.
SetupToken() The token of the setup link, <AdminPath>/setup?token=…, when the site started without accounts; empty otherwise. Every start makes a new one.
InviteAdministrator(ctx, email) Creates an administrator with a password nobody knows and returns a link, valid for an hour, where its owner chooses one: on BaseURL, or the path without it, such as /admin/reset-password?token=…. Needs Start (ErrNotStarted before it), also on a site with accounts. See Accounts and permissions.
Ready(ctx) The check behind /readyz: nil when the app has started, the database answers, every schema version this start applied is still in the database and the media storage can be reached, when it can tell (media.Pinger).
Metrics() An http.Handler that writes the app's metrics in the Prometheus text format, the same as /metrics. It answers 503 before Start.

A module key starts with a lowercase letter, followed by lowercase letters, digits or hyphens, up to 64 characters. accounts, groups, pages, media, site, login, logout, setup, forgot-password, reset-password, account, trash, assets, presence, theme, mail, partials and webthings are reserved.

Some modules also add admin sections named after their key, such as news-categories for a publishing instance news. A key equal to such a section stops Start with "admin section … exists twice: choose module keys that differ …".

Module packages offer a typed Of for Service, for example publishing.Of(app, "news"). After Start, the app's fields DB, Auth, Media, Site, Pages and Frontend give the core services, for example to fill an empty site, and Links the links between published content (see Pages):

if err := app.Start(ctx); err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

if err := seed(ctx, app); err != nil {
    _ = app.Close()
    log.Fatal(err)
}

// ListenAndServe sees that the app has started and only serves.
if err := app.ListenAndServe(ctx, ":8080"); err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

To serve with your own http.Server, for example with TLS, call Start, use the app as the handler and call Close when the server stops. See Deployment.

Guides.Title: Pages
Guides.Summary: Editors build the site's structure as a tree of pages in the admin. Each page has an address and a place in the menu, and shows either its own text or a module.
Guides.Body:
The page tree

Every page except the home page has a parent page. The tree gives each page its address:

Home                        /en/
├── About                   /en/about
│   └── Team                /en/about/team
└── News [module: news]     /en/news, and everything below it

Under Pages the admin shows this tree in the order of the menu: Home first, each page with its children indented below it. Every page shows its path, its module if it has one, and its status: Draft, In review, Published, Changes not published or Scheduled. A tab per language shows the tree in that language and marks pages that miss a translation there. New page opens an empty page below Home.

The ↑ and ↓ buttons move a page up or down among the pages with the same parent. A page can also be dragged by its handle to another place among them; a line shows where it lands, and Escape cancels. The order is not part of a revision: it changes the menu on the site at once. Pages that share a position, for example after an import, are in the order they were created, the same in every language. The buttons and handles need the right to edit pages and are hidden while the tree is searched. The buttons also work from the keyboard and without JavaScript.

A page has these fields:

Field Per language What it does
Title yes The page's name in the menu, in the layout's .Title and in search results. Required.
Web address yes The page's own part of its address, its slug, such as team. Made from the title when left empty.
Summary yes A short text: the layout's .Description, for the meta description, and the summary in search results.
Content yes The page's text, written formatted and stored as Markdown; see Editing and publishing.
Parent page no Where the page sits in the tree.
Shows on this page no A module instance that serves this page and everything below it, or "Nothing, a normal page".

The fields without a language are shared: changing the parent in one language moves the page in every language.

Addresses

A page's address is the language prefix followed by the slugs of its parents and its own slug, such as /nl/over-ons/team and /en/about/team. Every language has its own slugs.

  • A Web address uses lowercase letters, digits and dashes, and does not start or end with a dash. Another value is refused at the field: "Use lowercase letters, digits and dashes for the web address."
  • An empty Web address is made from the title when the page is saved: "Opening hours" becomes opening-hours, and -2, -3 and so on are added when a page with the same parent already uses it. A title without Latin letters or digits, such as one in Greek, needs a web address typed by hand; without one, saving is refused with "Give the page a web address of lowercase letters, digits and dashes, or a title it can be made from."
  • Within one language, pages with the same parent need different web addresses. This is checked when a page is published.
  • A top-level page cannot have the first segment of one of the app's own addresses as its web address: that of the admin path, admin by default, and media, assets, theme, healthz, readyz and metrics, and api while the content API is on. Publishing such a page is refused with "Another page at this level already uses this web address, or the address is reserved." A web address made from a title avoids them, such as theme-2 for "Theme".
  • A page is on the site in a language only when it and all its parent pages are published and have a title in that language. A page below an unpublished page is offline too.

To move a page, choose another Parent page and publish the page. The dropdown lists the pages in tree order, without the page itself, the pages below it and pages with a module. The page goes last among its new siblings, and its child pages move with it, so their addresses change too. The admin's tree shows the page under its new parent as soon as it is saved; the site's menu and addresses keep it in its old place until that revision is published. Until then, the page's editor shows the old and the new address in each language where it changes, and how many published items link to the old one, if any do. Once it is published, the old addresses answer "not found", unless the redirects module redirects them: with it, Publish this revision has a box, ticked by default, that redirects the old addresses of the page and of the pages below it to the new ones. A new Web address works the same way. See A new address.

Dragging a page in the tree to another parent does the same, without opening the page. Drop it onto a page to place it last below that page, or between the pages of another parent to place it there. The new parent is saved as a draft, and a message says to publish the page to move it on the site. The pages the dropdown leaves out take no drop, and the home page cannot be dragged.

The home page

The first start creates the home page, titled "Home" in every language, and publishes it. It is served at /<locale>/, such as /en/, and / redirects to the home page of the default language.

The home page is the root of the tree. It has no web address of its own and no parent, and it cannot show a module: its Parent page only offers "None (top level)" and its Shows on this page only "Nothing, a normal page". It always stays on the site; publish a newer revision to change it. Its editor has no Unpublish and no Move to trash, and its schedule only has Publish at. Other attempts are refused with "The home page always stays on the website: it cannot be unpublished, scheduled to be unpublished or deleted."

The home page is permanent by its nature, and nobody can take that away. Administrators can make other pages permanent too; see Permanent items.

Publishing and revisions

Pages are revisioned. Save draft creates a new draft revision; the published revision stays online until an editor publishes another one. A revision holds every language of the page, so publishing it publishes all its translations at once.

  • Publish this revision needs a title in the site's default language. When Site settings › Review is ticked for Pages, it also needs a reviewer's approval (see Review before publishing).
  • Unpublish asks "Take this off the website?" and takes the page offline, and with it every page below it. When published content links to the page, its editor lists that content and asks "Published items link to this page. Unpublish it anyway?" instead; with the redirects module it also offers Unpublish and redirect. See Links to a page.
  • Editors can preview a revision on the site, plan publication for later and restore an older revision.

Editing and publishing describes the publication box in detail.

Previewing a page

Preview this revision opens the page on the site with ?revision=<id>, such as /en/about/team?revision=…, in the language of the editor's tab. The page shows where the revision puts it: below the parent page's published address, with the revision's Web address. A published page also shows the revision at its current address, so a new web address or a page that was never published can be checked before publishing.

  • Only signed-in editors who may read Pages see the preview; everyone else gets the published page or "not found".
  • A page below a page that is not published has no address yet, so it cannot be previewed.
  • A page with a module shows that module's screen at the page's address, with the page as the revision has it.

See Previewing a revision for the banner and the headers.

Deleting a page

Move to trash asks "Move this item to the trash?" and moves a page to the trash, with its revisions. It leaves the menu and its address at once, and its web address and module are free for other pages. A page with child pages cannot be deleted: move or delete the child pages first. The home page cannot be deleted. When published content links to the page, the admin asks "Published items link to this page. Move it to the trash anyway?" instead.

A page comes back from the trash at its old place in the tree, published if it was. While its parent page is in the trash too, restore the parent first. Restoring refuses a published page whose web address another published page at its level uses now, or whose module is placed on another page now. Deleting a page for good in the trash removes its revisions too. See The trash.

Links to pages

Broken links, above the page tree, lists the addresses that links in published pages and module content lead to where the site has no page, with the reason and the content that links there. With the redirects module, each address has Create redirect. See Broken links.

From Go, App.Links, a links.Check, gives what the admin uses. Index(ctx) returns the links in published content: Index.Links() all of them, per language those of the pages first, in tree order, then those of the modules, and Index.To(addresses...) those to one of the addresses or below it, such as to /en/about and /en/about/team for /en/about, without the links in content that is there itself. Broken(ctx) returns the links to addresses where the site has no page and no redirect leads to a page or another website. Table(ctx) returns the published page table the links are resolved against, such as for the pages an address can redirect to. Each links.Link has the content it is in (Source), the key of that content's module (Module, empty for a page), its language (Locale), the link as written (Href), the address it leads to (Address, such as /en/contact, without query and fragment), the page that answers there (Page) and whether one does (Found). An address below a module page counts as found, as the module answers it, and so does the search screen. App.Links reads the published pages and the modules' Parts.Links only when it is asked, never while a visitor's page is served, and keeps what it found as the admin does (see Links to a page). The links in a published revision are kept per revision and language, since a revision never changes.

pages.Table.Lookup(locale, path) finds the published route of a path in a language without loading the page: the page at the path, or the module page above it, with the path below that page as rest, / for the page itself. ok is false when no published page answers. App.Pages.Table(ctx) returns the table of published routes:

table, err := app.Pages.Table(ctx)
if err != nil {
    return err
}

// With the news module on /news: route.Path is "/news", route.Module
// "news" and rest "/open-studio".
route, rest, ok := table.Lookup("en", "/news/open-studio")

The menu

The layout gets the published page tree in the current language as .Menu, a list of frontend.MenuItem:

Field Meaning
ID The page's ID.
Path The page's path without language prefix, such as /about/team.
Title The page's title in this language.
URL The page's address, such as /en/about/team.
Active The visitor is on this page or on a page below it.
Children The pages below it, with the same fields.

The menu starts below the home page, so Home itself is not in it; link to it with .Site.HomeURL. Pages are in the order of the admin's page tree, set with ↑ and ↓ or by dragging, except a page whose move to another parent is not published yet: it stays in its old place. Module pages are in the menu like any other page.

<nav>
    <a href="{{.Site.HomeURL}}">{{.Site.Name}}</a>
    {{range .Menu}}
        <a href="{{.URL}}" {{if .Active}}aria-current="page"{{end}}>{{.Title}}</a>
        {{with .Children}}
            <ul>
                {{range .}}<li><a href="{{.URL}}" {{if .Active}}aria-current="page"{{end}}>{{.Title}}</a></li>{{end}}
            </ul>
        {{end}}
    {{end}}
</nav>

Every published page is in the menu. To leave a page out, skip it in the layout by its Path, for example with {{if ne .Path "/privacy"}} inside {{range .Menu}}.

Placing a module on a page

The Shows on this page field lists the module instances from main.go that serve pages of their own. Choose one and publish the page: the module then serves the page's address and every address below it. With the publishing module on a page with the web address news:

Address Shows
/en/news the list of posts
/en/news/category/<slug> the posts in one category
/en/news/<slug> one post

Each module's README lists the addresses it serves and the templates it uses.

  • An instance can be placed on one page only.
  • A page with a module cannot have child pages.
  • Most bundled modules use the page's title as the title of their list. The page's Summary and Content are not shown on the module's screens, but the layout can show them from .Page.
  • {{moduleURL "news"}} is the address of the page an instance is placed on, in the current language, or empty when it is on no page.
  • When an instance is removed from main.go, its page stays published and answers with status 503 until the instance is back or the page is unpublished.

Using modules explains instances, keys and templates.

page.gohtml

page.gohtml shows a page without a module. It gets a frontend.Page:

Field Meaning
ID The page's ID.
ParentID The parent page's ID, empty for the home page.
Slug The page's own part of its path in this language, such as team.
Path The whole path without language prefix, such as /about/team; / for the home page.
Title The title.
Description The description.
Body The content, rendered from Markdown to HTML.
URL The page's address, such as /en/about/team.
IsHome Set for the home page, which sites often design differently. 
{{/* @dot github.com/donseba/go-webthings/frontend.Page */}}
<main id="content">
    {{if .IsHome}}
        <section class="hero">
            <h1>{{.Title}}</h1>
            {{with .Description}}<p class="lead">{{.}}</p>{{end}}
        </section>
        {{range posts "news" 3}}<a href="{{.URL}}">{{.Title}}</a>{{end}}
    {{else}}
        <h1>{{.Title}}</h1>
    {{end}}

    <div class="prose">{{.Body}}</div>
</main>

The layout gets the same page as .Page on content pages and their previews, and on module screens the page the module is placed on. Use {{with .Page}} in the layout, because the search and "not found" screens have no page there. A preview has the Path and URL of the address it is shown at, also for a page that was never published.

task templates -- site writes starting points for layout.gohtml, page.gohtml, 404.gohtml and search.gohtml. Templates explains how the layout and the content templates fit together.

404.gohtml

404.gohtml is shown, with status 404, for every address that does not exist:

  • an address without a known language prefix, such as /about (shown in the default language);
  • a path that no published page has;
  • an address below a module page that the module does not know, such as a post that was unpublished.

It gets a frontend.NotFound, with HomeURL the home page in the current language. The layout's .Title is "Not found", translated with the site's tl (msgid Not found). task translations finds that text itself, although no template contains it (see Languages). The menu is that of the current language and the language switch leads to the home page of each language.

{{/* @dot github.com/donseba/go-webthings/frontend.NotFound */}}
<main id="content">
    <h1>{{tl localizer "Page not found"}}</h1>
    <p><a href="{{.HomeURL}}">{{tl localizer "Back to the home page"}}</a></p>
</main>

Without 404.gohtml the site answers with a plain "404 page not found".

Canonical addresses

Every page has one address. Other spellings redirect to it, so search engines and visitors see one version:

Request Answer
/ 302 to the default language's home page, such as /en/
/en 301 to /en/
/en/about/ 301 to /en/about
/en//about or /en/./about 307 to /en/about: Go's http.ServeMux cleans the path
/EN/about 301 to /en/about, the language code as written in the site settings

A redirect keeps the query string: /en/about/?ref=mail leads to /en/about?ref=mail. Only the home page ends with a slash. Content pages answer GET and HEAD requests only.

Guides.Title: Languages
Guides.Summary: A site has one or more content languages. Every address starts with a language code, editors translate each page and module item, and the templates' own texts are translated in .po files.
Guides.Body:
Content languages

The first start takes the languages from Config.Locales:

app := webthings.New(webthings.Config{
    Name:    "Atelier Noord",
    Locales: locales.Config{Default: "nl", Enabled: []string{"nl", "en"}},
})

Without Locales the site starts in English only. After the first start the languages are part of the site settings and Config.Locales is ignored: editors change them under Site settings, in Default language, Languages and Other languages.

  • Languages has a checkbox for 47 common languages, each with its own name and its code, such as "Nederlands (nl)" or "Deutsch (de)", the same for every editor. A regional variant gets its language's name, such as "Português (pt-BR)", and a code without a known name is shown as the code. Enabled languages that are not among them get a checkbox too.
  • Other languages adds languages that are not listed, as codes separated by commas. Codes are language tags such as pt-BR or en-US; underscores are not allowed.
  • Default language offers every language of the list, so a language ticked in the same save can be the default. A default that is not ticked under Languages is refused at the field: "Tick the default language under Languages as well."
  • The language switch shows the languages in the order they were added: a new language comes last.

Addresses per language

Every address starts with a language code: /nl/over-ons and /en/about are the same page in two languages, each with its own slug. / redirects to the home page of the default language.

The code in the address is written as in the site settings; /EN/about redirects to /en/about. An address with a code that is not enabled, or without a code, is "not found". Pages lists all redirects.

Translating content

Every editor in the admin has a tab per language: pages, module items, media and the site settings. A tab names its language in that language, such as "Nederlands" or "Deutsch", with the code only where two languages share a name, such as "Português (pt)" and "Português (pt-BR)". Each tab shows the state of that language:

  • Translated: the item can be shown in this language.
  • Incomplete translation: some text exists, but not enough to show it.
  • Missing translation: nothing has been written yet.

The page tree and the overview of each module's items have a tab per language too. These tabs only name the language, since a whole list has no single state; instead, each item that is not complete in that language shows "Missing translation".

What makes a translation complete depends on the content. A page needs a title, and every page except Home also a Web address, which is made from the title when it is left empty; a news post needs a title and a web address, made from its title in the same way. Each module's README says what it needs.

  • Publishing needs a complete translation in the default language. The admin answers "Complete the default language before publishing." otherwise.
  • In other languages an item is shown once its translation is complete. Until then it is left out of lists, menus, search and sitemap.xml in that language.
  • A page is on the site in a language only when its parent pages are translated there too.
  • A revision of a page, post or event holds all its languages, so publishing it publishes every translation at once.

The site settings have their own texts per language: Site title, Tagline, SEO title, SEO description and Footer, which is formatted text like a page's content. Media files have a title and alt text per language; see Media and images.

Adding or removing a language

To add a language, tick it under Languages in the site settings, or write its code under Other languages, and save. Then:

  1. Fill in the site texts in the new language's tab of the site settings.
  2. Translate the home page and publish it. Every page of a language hangs below the home page, so /de/ is "not found" until the home page has a German title.
  3. Translate and publish the other pages and the module content.
  4. Add a .po file for the templates' texts (see below).

A language whose code is the first segment of the admin path, such as en with the admin at /en/admin, cannot be enabled: the admin would take its addresses. The site settings refuse it with "A language cannot have the code that one of the website's own addresses starts with, such as the admin's: its pages could not be reached.", and a start with such a language enabled stops with an error. While the content API is on, the code api cannot be enabled either.

Unticking a language takes its addresses offline. Its translations stay in the database and come back when the language is enabled again.

Changing the default language changes where / leads, and from then on publishing needs a complete translation in the new default language.

The language switch

The layout gets .Languages, a list of frontend.Language with Locale, URL, Active (the current language) and Default (the site's default language). It links to the same content in each language where that content is published:

  • on a page, to the same page in the languages it has;
  • on a module screen, to the same list or item, such as a post, in the languages it is translated in; a screen whose module gives no translations (frontend.Content.Alternates) links to the module's page in the other languages and to itself in its own language (see Search and SEO);
  • on the search screen, to the search in each language, keeping the query;
  • on "not found", to the home page of each language;
  • on a preview, as on the published page or item: a page's published languages, or a post's or event's translations.
<html lang="{{.Locale}}">
<head>
    {{slot "head"}}
</head>
<body>
    <nav aria-label="{{tl localizer "Language"}}">
        {{range .Languages}}
            <a href="{{.URL}}" hreflang="{{.Locale}}" lang="{{.Locale}}" {{if .Active}}aria-current="true"{{end}}>{{.Locale}}</a>
        {{end}}
    </nav>

Core's head tags, which {{slot "head"}} places (see The head region), link to the same content in each language with hreflang, and, when the content is in more than one language, to its address in the default language as hreflang="x-default", for visitors whose language the site does not have; sitemap.xml does the same. .Locale is the current language in the layout; other templates get it with {{locale}}. Search and SEO covers the alternate links.

Translating the templates' texts

The texts written in the templates themselves, such as "Read more" or "Back to the home page", are translated with gettext files. The starter loads them in main.go:

translations, err := frontend.Translations("translations")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

app := webthings.New(webthings.Config{
    Templates:    os.DirFS("templates"),
    Translations: translations,
})

frontend.Translations reads translations/<code>.po for every language, such as nl.po and en.po, and returns go-translator's *translator.Translator. In Config.Translations, it gives every template go-translator's four template functions; localizer is the page's language:

Function Use
{{tl localizer "Read more"}} a text
{{tl localizer "%d of %d" .Number .Total}} a text with values, in fmt style
{{tn localizer "%d comment" "%d comments" .Count .Count}} singular and plural, chosen by the number
{{ctl localizer "menu" "Home"}} a text with a context, for words that translate differently in different places
{{ctn localizer "menu" "%d item" "%d items" .Count .Count}} plural with a context

Core translates its own texts with the same files: the title of the 404 page, the heading and the message of the error page (see Templates), the names of social networks, the title of feeds, go-form's texts in visitor forms, and the names of months and days and the date patterns (see Dates, times and money). Without Config.Translations, every text shows as written. app.Frontend.SetTranslations sets the translations after Start, before the site serves.

Write the texts in English. A text without a translation is shown as written, so a new language works before its file exists. tn and ctn then show the singular when the number is 1 and the plural otherwise, as in English.

A page's language finds its file whatever the spelling: nl-BE uses nl_BE.po or nl-BE.po. A text that file lacks comes from the file of the language alone, nl.po, and then from another region of the same language, nl_NL.po first. So nl_BE.po only needs the texts that differ from nl.po, and a site with only nl_NL.po translates nl pages too. The file of another language is never used: German without a file of its own shows the texts as written. A file serves the language its name names, whatever its Language header says, so name each file by its language code: a file such as dutch.po serves no page.

go-form's texts in the visitor forms are translated with these files too, in the page's language. That includes go-form's own texts, such as the "(required)" that screen readers announce, and the messages a visitor's post with mistakes gets at its fields, such as "This field is required.", in the language of the page the form was on; see Visitor forms. One of go-form's own texts that the site's file does not translate shows in go-form's catalogue of the page's language, or of the language alone, such as nl for nl-BE. go-form brings English and Dutch, so nl and nl-BE pages show "Dit veld is verplicht." without an entry in nl.po; other languages show its texts in English. Nothing is added to the site's files. The files are read when the site starts: restart it after changing them.

Keeping the files up to date

The starter's Taskfile.yml has two tasks for this:

task translations          # write every text to translations/translations.pot
task translations:check    # list what each language misses
  1. task translations scans every template of every theme, plus the default templates, components and e-mail of the modules and core that not every theme replaces, and writes their texts to translations/translations.pot. It adds the texts core translates in Go, with core:texts as their reference: "Not found", the title of the 404 page, "Something went wrong. Please try again.", the message of the error page (see Templates), the status texts of its heading ("Not Found", "Too Many Requests", "Internal Server Error" and "Service Unavailable"), the title of the feeds, "%[1]s from %[2]s", and the names of the social networks. It adds the names of months and days and the date patterns, with their contexts, as core:calendar (see Dates, times and money). When a template uses form_open, form_field or form_render, it also adds the labels, help texts, placeholders, option labels, submit texts and messages of the modules' visitor forms (Module.Forms), as module:<type>/forms. It prints how many texts it wrote, from how many templates.
  2. Open a language's .po file in Poedit, choose Translation › Update from POT File… and pick translations/translations.pot. For a new language, create its file from the same POT file.
  3. Translate the new texts, save and restart the site.

task translations:check lists the texts each .po file still misses, or has with an empty translation, and fails when any are missing, so it can run in CI. task translations:check -- --csv writes the list as CSV for a spreadsheet.
