Called before Back, env.Frontend.KeepForm(w, r, key, model, errs) also keeps the post for that page: the form that frontend.VisitorForm makes there for the same key and action then shows the visitor's values again, with go-form's messages at the fields that need a correction. model is the input the post was read into, a go-form form.Schema, or the form VisitorForm made, and errs are the errors to show, such as those of BindForm. A post refused for another reason passes nil and shows its values alone. The handler in A form of your own keeps its post this way, and so do the comments, newsletter, registrations (sign-up and cancel) and submissions modules. They still return their result, such as ?newsletter=invalid, for the notice above the form. A kept post changed nothing on the site, and KeepForm says so (frontend.NothingChanged), so the site's output cache keeps its pages; see Caching and testing a module.

Templates need no change: form_field and form_render with nil as their errors show the kept post. This works without JavaScript and with HTMX, which follows the redirect and swaps in the form as the page renders it. A form in a fragment that loads after the page, placed with deferredSlot, does not show the kept post: the request for the page takes it before the fragment's own request comes. Place such a form with slot or requiredSlot.

The post waits on the server, in core's table wt_kept_form, for five minutes at most. The visitor gets a cookie for the form's page only, wt_form_<key> (frontend.KeptFormCookie followed by the key), that holds a random token and nothing else. The table keeps the token's SHA-256, not the token, so its rows do not give away the posts that wait. The cookie is HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax, Secure when the request came over HTTPS, and lasts five minutes. The kept post holds only the values of the form's own fields, never passwords, files or the spam trap, and at most 128 KiB in all; a larger post keeps its messages and leaves out its longest values. The first GET of the page with the cookie takes the post, which removes it, and clears the cookie, so the post shows once; a prefetch leaves it for the visit itself. A token that is unknown, older than five minutes, or kept for another form or page shows nothing and changes nothing about the answer. A page view that takes a kept post is sent with Cache-Control: private, no-store, and the site's output cache neither answers nor keeps a request with such a cookie (see Caching and testing a module), so no cache keeps the visitor's values. One visitor, known by a hash of their address, has at most ten posts kept at a time; a newer post removes the oldest. Posts nobody came back for are removed when other posts are kept, and every hour. When the form was on no page of the site, nothing is kept and the visitor returns with the result alone.

When several forms on a page share the key and the action, such as a comment form below each post, only the one whose hidden fields hold the posted values, here the post's ID in subject, shows the post.

With HTMX

A form can also post with HTMX and update only its own part of the page. Put the form in a fragment of the theme named after the module instance, such as fragments/remarks.gohtml with the id remarks, and aim it at the fragment. form_open takes more attributes after the model, as name and value pairs or as submitAttrs writes them:

{{with commentInput "remarks" .ID}}
    {{form_open . "class" "comment-form" (submitAttrs runtime (commentURL "remarks") "target" "#remarks" "swap" "outerHTML")}}
        {{form_field . "subject" nil}}
        {{form_field . "name" nil}}
        {{form_field . "body" nil}}
        <button type="submit">{{tl localizer "Post comment"}}</button>
    {{form_close}}
{{end}}

A class adds to the form theme's class, here wt-form comment-form. The subject field is hidden and holds the post's ID. submitAttrs writes hx-post, hx-target and hx-swap; see Template functions. The module redirects as above, the browser follows with the same target, and the page answers with the fragment alone, now with the result. Without JavaScript the same form posts and returns the usual way, to the same element, #remarks. A poll is not a fragment of its own, so its form aims at its .Anchor and picks that element out of the page with hx-select. See HTMX.

Throttling

frontend.Limits puts a module's limits around its visitor actions, always in the same order: first the size of the request body, then how often each visitor may post. It is middleware for the routes of the module's action router, env.Actions():

actions := env.Actions()

actions.Use(frontend.Limits(env.Key, frontend.ActionLimits{
    Body:   64 << 10,
    Posts:  5,
    Window: 10 * time.Minute,
}))
actions.Post("/post", post).As("post")

actions.Use comes before the routes and limits all of them. To limit one route only, add the limits to that route: actions.Post("/subscribe", subscribe).Use(frontend.Limits(…)). The newsletter module limits only its signups this way, since one-click unsubscribes come from a few mail providers' servers. frontend.Actions(key, handler, limits) puts the same limits around any other handler.

Body is the largest request body in bytes. It can only lower the site's limit for actions (see A form of your own), which applies first: a larger Body has no effect, and zero keeps the site's limit. Each visitor may post Posts times per Window; zero posts or a zero Window means no throttling, and GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE requests are not counted. A visitor over the limit returns to the form with the result throttled (frontend.ResultThrottled), so the page can say so. A Throttled handler answers them another way instead. The counts are kept in memory: a restart clears them, and several servers each count their own posts.

frontend.Throttle(limit, window, handler) throttles without the body limit, and answers 429 Too Many Requests over the limit, or with the handler of frontend.OnLimit. A limit or window of zero does not throttle. The throttling is go-router's middleware.RateLimit.

The bundled modules use these limits per visitor:

Module Posts
comments 5 per 10 minutes
forms 10 per 10 minutes
newsletter 20 signups per hour
polls 20 votes per minute
registrations 10 per 10 minutes
submissions 5 per hour

Cross-site protection

Posts to /_/ from another site are refused with 403 Forbidden (Go's http.CrossOriginProtection). Browsers tell where a post comes from in the Sec-Fetch-Site and Origin headers, so this needs no token or cookie: a form never expires, and pages with forms can be cached. A form on another subdomain of your domain counts as another site.

The protection stops other websites from posting in a visitor's name. Scripts that post directly send no such headers and pass; the spam trap and throttling deal with them.

Knowing the visitor

frontend.ClientIP(r) is the visitor's IP address. Throttling and the stats use it.

env.VisitorID(ctx, r, parts...) tells visitors apart without storing their address: an HMAC-SHA256 of the parts and the address, keyed with the instance's visitors secret, as 64 hexadecimal digits. It differs per module instance, and nobody can find the address from it by trying them all. With the date as a part, time.Now().UTC().Format(time.DateOnly), it changes every day. The polls use it, next to a cookie, for one vote per visitor, and the comments keep a daily one with each message.

Behind a reverse proxy, every request comes from the proxy. List it in Config.TrustedProxies, as IP addresses or CIDR ranges:

app := webthings.New(webthings.Config{
    TrustedProxies: []string{"127.0.0.1", "10.0.0.0/8"},
})

Only requests from these addresses have their X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP and Forwarded headers believed. X-Forwarded-For is read from the right, skipping trusted proxies; the first other address is the visitor, so a visitor cannot pose as another address by sending the header themselves. X-Real-IP is used when there is no X-Forwarded-For, and the for= entries of Forwarded (RFC 7239) when there is neither, read like X-Forwarded-For. The visitor's address also replaces r.RemoteAddr, with port 0, such as 198.51.100.7:0. The X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Host headers of these proxies also give the site's address, or else the proto= and host= of their Forwarded, for absolute links when Config.BaseURL is empty.

Without the setting the headers are ignored, since anyone can send them. Behind a proxy that means all visitors share one address, and the throttles count them together. See Deployment.

A form of your own

A site adds its own form with a small module that registers a visitor action on its action router, env.Actions(), as the bundled modules do. This one takes "call me back" requests at /_/callback/request:

// CallbackInput is the form of a "call me back" request: a phone number on
// one line, at most 50 characters.
type CallbackInput struct {
    Phone string `form:"input,tel" name:"phone" label:"Phone" required:"true" maxLength:"50" line:"true" autocomplete:"tel"`
}

func callback() webthings.Module {
    // actions is the module's action router, from Setup.
    var actions *router.Router

    return webthings.Module{
        Type: "callback",
        Key:  "callback",
        // The form's label, for task translations.
        Forms: []any{CallbackInput{}},
        Funcs: template.FuncMap{
            // {{callbackForm}} is the form: it posts to the action named
            // request and returns the visitor to the element with the id callback.
            "callbackForm": func(ctx context.Context) form.RenderModel {
                return frontend.VisitorForm(ctx, CallbackInput{}, actions.RoutePath("request"), "callback")
            },
            // {{callbackResult}} is the result in the page's address, such as "sent";
            // "" for a result the module does not know.
            "callbackResult": func(ctx context.Context) string {
                if r := frontend.Request(ctx); r != nil {
                    return frontend.Result(r, "callback", "sent", "invalid", frontend.ResultThrottled)
                }

                return ""
            },
        },
        Setup: func(env webthings.Env) (webthings.Parts, error) {
            actions = env.Actions()

            // At most 16 KiB per post, and 5 posts per visitor per 10 minutes.
            actions.Use(frontend.Limits("callback", frontend.ActionLimits{
                Body:   16 << 10,
                Posts:  5,
                Window: 10 * time.Minute,
            }))
            actions.Post("/request", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
                if frontend.IsSpam(r) {
                    frontend.Back(w, r, "callback", "sent")

                    return
                }

                var in CallbackInput

                errs, err := env.Frontend.BindForm(r, &in)
                if err != nil || len(errs) > 0 {
                    env.Frontend.KeepForm(w, r, "callback", in, errs)
                    frontend.Back(w, r, "callback", "invalid")

                    return
                }

                // Store in.Phone, or mail it to the office (see mail.md).

                frontend.Back(w, r, "callback", "sent")
            }).As("request")

            return webthings.Parts{}, nil
        },
    }
}

router is go-router and form is go-form (github.com/donseba/go-form/v2). Add the module with app.Use(callback()), and show the form in any template:

{{$form := callbackForm}}
{{$result := callbackResult}}
<div id="callback">
    {{if eq $result "sent"}}<p>{{tl localizer "Thank you. We will call you soon."}}</p>{{end}}
    {{if eq $result "invalid"}}<p>{{tl localizer "Please enter your phone number."}}</p>{{end}}
    {{if eq $result "throttled"}}<p>{{tl localizer "Please try again later."}}</p>{{end}}

    {{form_open $form}}
        {{form_field $form "phone" nil}}
        <button type="submit">{{tl localizer "Call me back"}}</button>
    {{form_close}}
</div>

env.Actions() is a go-router mounted at /_/<key>/, so its routes are relative to that and become part of the site's routes. A handler sees the whole path, such as /_/callback/request, and r.PathValue gives the route's wildcards. A path without a route gets a plain 404, and a path that only has routes for other methods, such as a GET of /_/callback/request, gets 405. Route names are shared by the whole site, and a module may run more than once, so core puts the key in front: the route named request is callback.request on the site. The module asks its own router by the short name: actions.RoutePath("request") is /_/callback/request, and actions.RoutePathArgs fills in wildcards and adds a query. This needs no request, so it also gives the links in e-mail (see E-mail).

frontend.VisitorForm(ctx, model, action, key) makes the form of model for the templates: it posts to action, carries the spam trap, and has the page being rendered with #<key> as its back field, as in The hidden fields. The field of the example has the id callback-phone.

Core adds the cross-site protection to every action, and limits the request body to 1 MiB (webthings.DefaultActionBodyLimit); Parts.ActionBodyLimit sets another limit, for example for uploads. The example sets a lower limit of its own in ActionLimits, as the bundled modules do; a higher Body there has no effect, so a module that takes more raises Parts.ActionBodyLimit instead.

env.Frontend.BindForm(r, &in) reads the post into CallbackInput and checks it against the tags, as the bundled modules do: here a phone number that is not empty, at most 50 characters and one line, without tabs, line breaks or other control characters. It trims the spaces around text and reads line breaks as \n, as browsers count them for maxlength. A value that cannot be read as its field's type, such as abc for a number, is an error of that field with the rule invalid. Every error names the rule it broke (form.FieldValidationError.Rule), for a module that answers with a result per rule. err is only set when the post cannot be read at all. The messages are in the language of the page the form was on (BackLocale), translated with the site's translations. env.Frontend.KeepForm then keeps a post with mistakes for that page, so the form shows the number and its message again there; see A post with mistakes. The same tags give the theme's field its required, maxlength and autocomplete, and Forms lets task translations find its label when a template uses form_open, form_field or form_render. Writing a module covers storage and the rest of a module, and The admin of a module its admin sections.

An e-mail address that mail will go to gets validate:"mail" (mail.Rule) next to form:"input,email", as the bundled modules' e-mail fields do: it refuses an address that mail cannot reach, such as one without a dot; see E-mail. A form:"input,datetime-local" field is read and shown in the site's timezone, as in the admin, so a visitor enters the site's local time; see The admin of a module.

When something else fails, such as storing the post, the handler answers with env.Frontend.Fail(w, r, err), as the bundled modules do. It logs the error with the module's key and answers with status 500 and the theme's 500.gohtml, in the language of the form's page and with the theme's asset versions, as its pages render. Without a 500.gohtml, go-partial's plain error page answers, with its heading and message translated and the page's language as its lang; see Templates. An HTMX post gets the same page, which the client shows as the whole page with reloadOnError; see HTMX.

Forms built by editors

The forms module lets editors build contact forms and other forms in the admin, with an inbox and a notification mail. Its posting differs from the visitor actions above:

  • The form is shown on the page the instance is placed on, and posts to that same page (.Action), not to /_/.
  • With errors, the page shows the form again at once, with the visitor's answers and an error per field (status 422). There is no redirect, so it needs no KeepForm.
  • After a valid post the visitor returns to the page with ?sent=1.
  • .Form is the form as the editor built it, which a theme renders with {{form_render .Form .Errors}}, or with form_open and form_field for each name in .Fields. Both write the spam trap; there is no back field, because the form returns to its own page.
  • Over the limit, the form is shown again with .Throttled set and the answers kept (status 429).
  • An email field takes one address mail can be sent to (mail.Rule), as the e-mail fields of the other forms do, since a reply to the notification goes to it. The module sets the rule with go-form's Spec.Validate.

Cross-site protection, the spam trap and throttling work the same way, so the form also needs no token and never expires.

Next steps

  • E-mail covers the confirmations and notifications that forms send.
  • Using modules lists the modules with visitor forms.
  • Writing a module explains Parts and the module's Setup.

Guides.Title: E-mail
Guides.Summary: Modules send e-mail through one sender that the site configures: confirmations to visitors and notifications to staff. The texts come from templates that a theme can replace and translate.
Guides.Body:
Choose a sender

Config.Mail is the sender. Without one, messages are written to the log instead of sent, which suits development:

INFO mail not sent (no sender configured) to=anna@example.com subject="Please confirm your subscription" text=…

SMTP

mail.SMTP sends through a mail server:

app := webthings.New(webthings.Config{
    Mail: mail.SMTP{
        Host:     "smtp.example.com",
        Port:     587,
        Username: os.Getenv("SMTP_USERNAME"),
        Password: os.Getenv("SMTP_PASSWORD"),
        From:     "Atelier Noord <website@example.com>",
    },
})
  • Port defaults to 587. STARTTLS is used when the server offers it, as on ports 587 and 25. Implicit TLS on port 465 is not supported.
  • With a Username, the sender signs in with PLAIN authentication. Go only sends the password over an encrypted connection, or to localhost.
  • From is an address, optionally with a name.
  • Timeout bounds one message, from connecting to the end of the conversation; it defaults to 30 seconds (mail.DefaultSMTPTimeout). Sending also stops when its context ends.

Log and Memory

mail.Log{} is what the site uses without a sender. Give it a Logger to write elsewhere than the default slog logger.

mail.Memory keeps the messages, for tests:

outbox := &mail.Memory{}

app := webthings.New(webthings.Config{Mail: outbox})

// … sign up for the newsletter …

for _, message := range outbox.Sent() {
    t.Log(message.To, message.Subject)
}

A test site started with sitetest collects its mail in Site.Mail, a mail.Memory. Site.Mails(n) waits until the site has sent n messages, for mail sent in the background.

Other providers

Any type with this method can send:

type Sender interface {
    Send(ctx context.Context, message mail.Message) error
}

A mail.Message has To, ReplyTo, Subject, Text (always set) and HTML (optional). Headers holds extra header fields, such as List-Unsubscribe on newsletters; pass them on. mail.Compose(from, message) writes a message as RFC 5322 bytes, for providers that take raw mail, and refuses header names it writes itself and values with line breaks. See mail.go.

A sender can also say how it sends, for whoever checks the site's set-up, by implementing mail.Describer:

type Describer interface {
    Describe() string
}

The setup guide's E-mail step shows the description after "The site sends e-mail with". mail.SMTP describes itself with its server, port and From address, such as SMTP mail.example.com:587, from Site <noreply@example.com>, without the username and password. mail.Log and mail.Memory implement it too, but for mail.Log, and without a sender, the step says "No sender configured: e-mail is written to the server log, not sent." Never put a secret, such as a password or an API key, in a description. A sender without the method shows as "The site sends e-mail with the sender its code sets." See Mail and storage.

The mailjet package of go-webthings-contrib (github.com/donseba/go-webthings-contrib/mailjet) sends through Mailjet's API. Its sender's From must be an address Mailjet has validated.

What sends e-mail

Apart from the admin's password reset link, its messages to reviewers and the test e-mail of the setup guide's E-mail step, core sends no e-mail of its own. These modules do:

Module Mail To Language
comments notify the notification address in its settings admin
forms notify the form's notification address admin
newsletter confirmation a new subscriber the subscriber's
registrations confirmation, cancellation the visitor who signed up the visitor's
submissions notify the notification address admin
submissions received, accepted, rejected the sender, when the settings ask for it the sender's

Notifications have the visitor as Reply-To when they gave an address, so replying answers them. Registration mail has the e-mail address of Site settings as Reply-To.

Newsletter mailings are not templates: they are the editor's message, the mailing footer and a personal unsubscribe link, sent in the background. The message and the footer are Markdown. The HTML part shows them formatted, with the link at the end of the footer's last paragraph, so a footer ending in "Unsubscribe:" reads on into it; the text part holds the Markdown as written, with the media library's files as links.

In a mailing, images from the media library are not the uploads. Each is a copy at most 1200 pixels wide (media.MailImageWidth) and never larger than the upload, as a JPEG, or as a PNG for a PNG with transparency, since not every mail program shows WebP. Other images, such as a GIF, keep their own address. The HTML gives each image its size as width and height, so a mail program does not show it larger, and an image without a description in the Markdown gets the library's alt text in the mailing's language, or in the subscriber's for a mailing to every language. The text part shows such an image as a link, [alt](address), and a link to a file of the library with the file's address.

A message is sent while the request that causes it is handled, such as the visitor's post. A visitor who leaves early does not stop it; the sender's timeout still bounds it. A message that cannot be sent is logged; what the visitor sent is stored either way.

The admin sends its password reset link itself, through Config.Mail and in the background: plain text in the admin's language, without a template. See Accounts and permissions. Where the site asks for a review, it mails the reviewers the same way when a revision waits for them, under the same conditions as the reset link; see Editing and publishing.

Mail templates

A module declares its mail like its page templates, with English default texts. A theme replaces one with a file of its own, looked up in this order:

  1. mail/<key>/<name>.gohtml, for one instance, such as mail/remarks/notify.gohtml;
  2. mail/<type>/<name>.gohtml, for every instance of the module, such as mail/comments/notify.gohtml;
  3. the module's default.

Like other templates, a theme without the file uses the one in templates/default/. task templates -- <key> writes the module's defaults into templates/default/mail/<key>/ as a starting point, next to its page templates.

A mail template defines its parts:

{{/* @dot github.com/donseba/go-webthings/modules/comments.NotifyView */}}
{{define "subject"}}{{tl localizer "New message from"}} {{.Name}}{{end}}

{{define "text"}}
{{.Name}}{{with .Email}} <{{.}}>{{end}} {{tl localizer "wrote"}}:

{{.Body}}

{{tl localizer "Review:"}} {{.ReviewURL}}
{{template "mail/partials/signature.gohtml" .}}
{{end}}

{{define "html"}}
<p><strong>{{.Name}}</strong> {{tl localizer "wrote"}}:</p>
<blockquote>{{.HTML}}</blockquote>
<p><a href="{{.ReviewURL}}">{{tl localizer "Review"}}</a></p>
{{end}}
  • subject is required; its spaces and line breaks become single spaces.
  • text is required: the plain-text message, trimmed.
  • html is optional. When present, the message has both parts.
  • Each part renders through go-partial as a part of the theme's pages, with the same functions and render stages. subject and text are plain text (go-partial's RenderText, with Go's text/template), so nothing in them is HTML-escaped; html is escaped as on the pages.
  • Templates in the theme's mail/partials/ can be used in every mail template, by their path. The example expects templates/default/mail/partials/signature.gohtml.

Every template function works, in the language of the message: tl with the site's translations, date, time, money and the modules' functions. moduleURL, image and asset give addresses without the domain, so use the absolute links that the mail's data gives, such as .ReviewURL above.

Mail templates are read once and kept, like the theme's pages: a mail template that is changed or added while the site runs is used after a restart, or at once with Config.ReloadTemplates.

The default texts use tl, so the site's translations translate them without a template of your own. task translations collects their texts with those of your templates. See Languages.

Language

Mail to visitors is written in their language: the language of the page they used, or the one stored with their subscription or proposal.

Mail to staff, such as notifications, is written in Config.AdminLanguage, the language of the admin: English (en) unless the site sets another. Its texts are translated with the site's translation for that language, translations/<code>.po.

Links in e-mail

Links in e-mail must be absolute. Modules make them absolute with Config.BaseURL:

app := webthings.New(webthings.Config{
    BaseURL: "https://www.example.com",
})

Without a BaseURL, links use the address of the request that caused the mail: its Host header, and https when the connection is TLS. Behind a proxy listed in Config.TrustedProxies, the proxy's X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Host headers name the address instead, or else the proto= and host= of its Forwarded header; from other clients they are ignored. Set BaseURL in production, so every link points to the site's real address. Newsletter mailings use the site's address at the moment the editor sends them, for their links and images: every address of the site in a mailing is absolute, in the HTML and the text part, and relative links lead from the home page of the mailing's language, or of the subscriber's for a mailing to every language.

The admin's password reset is the exception: without a BaseURL it is not offered, since a link made from the Host header could point to another site. Config.Insecure allows it for local development.

Mail from your own module

A site's own module declares its mail in Module.Mail and sends it with Frontend.SendMail:

type RequestMail struct {
    Phone string
}

const requestMail = `{{define "subject"}}{{tl localizer "Call-back request"}}{{end}}

{{define "text"}}
{{tl localizer "Please call"}} {{.Phone}}.
{{end}}
`

func callback() webthings.Module {
    return webthings.Module{
        Type: "callback",
        Key:  "callback",
        Mail: []frontend.Template{{Name: "request", Data: RequestMail{}, Example: requestMail}},
        // Forms, Funcs and Setup …
    }
}

The module is the one from Visitor forms. The Example is the default text; a theme replaces it with mail/callback/request.gohtml. In the module's action handler, after env.Frontend.BindForm read the post into in:

_ = env.Frontend.SendMail(r.Context(), env.Mail, frontend.Letter{
    Locale: env.AdminLanguage,
    Key:    env.Key,
    Name:   "request",
    Data:   RequestMail{Phone: in.Phone},
    To:     []string{"office@example.com"},
})

Frontend.SendMail writes the mail with its template and sends it, as the bundled modules do. A visitor who leaves early does not cancel it; the sender's timeout still bounds it. A failure is logged with the module and the mail's name, and returned for a handler that tells the visitor; most ignore it. ReplyTo in the Letter sets where answers go, such as the visitor who wrote. env.Mail is always set: it logs when the site has no sender.

Pass the visitor's language for mail to visitors, such as env.Frontend.BackLocale(r), the language of the form's page. Pass env.AdminLanguage for mail to staff; it is "en" unless Config.AdminLanguage says otherwise. env.AbsoluteURL(r, path) makes a link absolute with BaseURL, or with the request's address.

A link to one of the module's own actions, such as a confirmation link, comes from its action router, env.Actions(), by route name. For a route named confirm, actions.RoutePathArgs("confirm", url.Values{"token": {token}}) is /_/<key>/confirm?token=…, as the newsletter module builds the links in its mail. This needs no request, so it also works for mail that is sent outside a visitor's request, such as a newsletter mailing.

Frontend.Mail(ctx, locale, key, name, data) only writes the message: the subject, text and HTML. The caller then sets the recipients and sends it.

A module that mails Markdown with media, such as a message an editor wrote, resolves the media as the newsletter does in ../modules/newsletter/sending.go. It renders the HTML part with markdown.Render and markdown.Options, whose Images gives each image as Frontend.MailImage(ctx, id) returns it, with its Width and Height, and Frontend.AltText(ctx, id, locale) when the Markdown gives no description. markdown.PlainMedia(source, options) writes the text part: the Markdown with every image as a link, [alt](address), and every link to a file with the file's address. Options.Base makes the addresses absolute in both parts. It is the absolute address that relative links lead from, such as the home page of the message's language, https://example.com/en/: every link and image address without a scheme is resolved from it as a browser resolves it, /en/about and about alike, and so are the paths that MailImage and MediaURL give when the library serves the file. Addresses with a scheme, such as https: and mailto:, and a #fragment alone stay as they are, and so does everything in code; an empty Base, or one that is not absolute, changes nothing.

Addresses in forms

A form field for an address that mail will go to gets validate:"mail", the rule mail.Rule, which visitor forms and the admin's forms check with mail.FormRule:

type SignupInput struct {
    Email string `form:"input,email" name:"email" label:"E-mail address" required:"true" maxLength:"254" autocomplete:"email" validate:"mail"`
}

It refuses an address that mail.Valid refuses. Valid takes a single plain address with a dot in it, since mail goes to addresses on the internet, so anna@localhost gets go-form's message for an invalid e-mail address at its field. An empty value passes; required:"true" checks that. An address that an e-mail input refuses on its own gets one message, not two. The bundled modules' e-mail fields use the rule, in visitor forms and in the admin, and so do the email fields editors build in the forms module. A field of a go-form form.Schema, such as those, names the rule in form.Spec.Validate, as the validate tag does for a field of a struct, and env.Frontend.ValidateSchema checks it.

Next steps

  • Visitor forms explains the forms that cause most mail.
  • Themes covers the theme folders that hold mail templates.
  • Writing a module covers Module.Mail and Env.

Guides.Title: Editing and publishing
Guides.Summary: Editors write formatted text that is stored as Markdown, keep drafts next to the published version and publish now or at a planned time. When they are signed in, the site itself shows them a link to edit what they look at.
Guides.Body:
Writing text

Text fields such as a page's Content or a post's Content show the text formatted, with a toolbar above it, and store it as Markdown. The toolbar has paragraph, headings 2 to 4, bold, italic, code, link, bulleted and numbered lists, quote, code block, horizontal line, an image from the media library, undo and redo. Pointing at a button shows its name and shortcut.

  • Link asks for an address, such as https://example.com, /en/contact or mailto:info@example.com. An empty address removes the link. Without selected text, the address becomes the link's text.
  • Image from the media library opens the library's images, with a search by file name, title and alternative text that ignores case and accents. Choose one, add an alternative text if you like, and press Insert, or double-click the image. The image gets a paragraph of its own and is stored as ![alt](media:<id>). The button is only there for editors who may read Media.
  • Pasted text keeps only what the toolbar offers. Fonts, colours and layout from Word or web pages are left out, and so are images pasted from elsewhere; HTML never gets into the text.
Keys Mac Does
Ctrl+B, Ctrl+I, Ctrl+` Cmd+B, Cmd+I, Cmd+` bold, italic, code
Ctrl+K Cmd+K link
Ctrl+Z Cmd+Z undo
Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y Cmd+Shift+Z or Cmd+Y redo
Ctrl+Shift+0 Control+Shift+0 paragraph
Ctrl+Shift+2, 3 or 4 Control+Shift+2, 3 or 4 heading 2, 3 or 4; again for a paragraph
Ctrl+Shift+7, Ctrl+Shift+8 Control+Shift+7, Control+Shift+8 numbered list, bulleted list
Ctrl+[, Ctrl+] Cmd+[, Cmd+] move a list item out, in
Shift+Enter Shift+Enter line break within a paragraph

Typed at the start of a line, some Markdown becomes formatting at once: ## , ### or #### a heading, - or * a bulleted list, 1. a numbered list, > a quote, ``` a code block and --- a horizontal line. Backspace right after it undoes it. Other Markdown typed in the formatted text, such as **bold**, stays plain text.

The Markdown view

The Markdown button at the end of the toolbar shows the text as Markdown, to write it by hand; pressing it again shows the formatted text. The browser remembers the choice for the next text. Without JavaScript the field is a plain box for Markdown.

The site understands Markdown with the GitHub additions: tables, strikethrough, task lists, and web addresses that become links by themselves. The formatted view cannot show tables and task lists (- [ ] item): a text with one opens in the Markdown view, with a note, and stays there.

## Opening hours

We are open from **Tuesday to Saturday**. See the [workshops](/en/workshops).

| Day      | Hours       |
| -------- | ----------- |
| Tuesday  | 10:00–17:00 |
| Saturday | 10:00–16:00 |
  • Raw HTML is left out, never rendered, so editors cannot break the page or add scripts.
  • Headings get an id made of their words, so [hours](#opening-hours) links to the heading above.
  • Templates get the text as HTML, such as {{.Body}} in page.gohtml.

The rendering is in the markdown package; modules render their own Markdown with Frontend.Markdown. The site keeps rendered texts in memory, up to 32 MB, so a text is not rendered again for every visit. A text with media is rendered again when the media library changes, and after a minute at most, so changes made on other servers show too.

How the text is saved

A text that is not changed is saved exactly as it was, and so is text changed in the Markdown view. Once a text is changed in the formatted view, the editor writes all of it in one style:

  • *italic* and **bold**, also where the text had _italic_ and __bold__;
  • numbered lists as 1., 2., 3., counting up from the first number, also where the text had 1);
  • headings with #, code blocks between ``` and horizontal lines as ---;
  • characters that would mean Markdown, such as a * typed as text, with a \ before them.

Images and files in the text

The Image from the media library button places an image. For other files, and for the Markdown view, every file in Media has a Use in content field with a ready-made reference:

![Bowls drying on the shelf](media:0192f3a4-5b6c-7d8e-9f01-23456789abcd)
[price-list.pdf](media:0192f3a4-5b6c-7d8e-9f01-23456789abce)

An image is written with its alt text in the language of the media screen's tab; any other file becomes a link. Paste the reference in the Markdown view: in the formatted view it stays plain text. The reference is turned into the file's address when the page is shown, so the text never holds the address itself.

  • Saving refuses a reference to a file that no longer exists or is in the trash: "A referenced media file no longer exists."
  • A file that content refers to, also in an older revision or from content in the trash, cannot be deleted from the library.
  • JPEG and PNG images in the text are shown as resized WebP copies, at most 1600 pixels wide, with copies in other widths for small and high-density screens. Media and images has the details.
  • An image written without alt text, such as ![](media:…), gets the media library's alternative text in the page's language.

Drafts and revisions

Pages and the content of the publishing and events modules are revisioned. Saving never changes the live site: it creates a new revision, a draft. The editor's button reads Save draft, and the admin says "Saved as a draft. Publish it to show it on the website." The published revision stays online until an editor publishes another one.

A revision holds every language of the item. Each language has its own tab in the editor; saving a tab creates a new revision with that language changed and the others as they were.

The overview shows each item's status:

Status Meaning
Draft No revision is published.
Published The newest revision is the published one.
Changes not published A newer draft exists next to the published revision.
Scheduled A publication is planned.
In review The newest revision waits for a reviewer; see Review before publishing.

The publication box

The editor of an item has a column on the right, beside the form: the Publication box, the box of a permanent item and Move to trash. The column stays in view while the form scrolls, and so does the form's save button. On a narrow screen the column comes below the form.

For revisioned content, the Publication box shows the selected, the latest and the published revision, and offers:

  • Publish this revision makes the selected revision public. It needs a complete translation in the site's default language: "Complete the default language before publishing." Where the site asks for a review, it also needs a reviewer's approval; see Review before publishing.
  • Unpublish takes the item offline, after the question "Take this off the website?". Its revisions are kept. For a page that published content links to, the admin asks another question; see Links to a page.
  • Preview this revision opens it on the website in a new tab; see Previewing a revision.
  • Schedule this revision plans publishing and unpublishing; see below. For a permanent item, such as the home page, it plans publishing only; see Permanent items.
  • Revision history lists every revision with its time, author and note, and its review state where the site asks for a review. The times are in the site's timezone, shown next to the heading. Open one to see it in the editor, preview it or publish it as it is. Restore as new draft copies it into a new revision on top, without publishing it.

Who may do what is set per section in the groups' permission matrix: an editor with the right to edit but not to publish can write drafts, and someone with the right to publish puts them online. Where the site asks for a review, a reviewer approves them first. An editor with only the read right sees the editor read-only, with the note "You can view this item but not change it." See Accounts and permissions.

Previewing a revision

A preview shows a revision on the website itself, in the site's design, at its own address with ?revision=<id>, such as /en/news/open-studio?revision=…. It opens in the language of the editor's tab and works for content that was never published too.

  • Only editors who are signed in and may read the section see it. For everyone else, and for a revision of other content than the address shows, ?revision= does nothing: the address shows the published page or "not found", so it never tells that a revision exists.
  • A page shows at its published address, or where the revision would put it: below its parent page's published address, with the revision's Web address. A post or an event shows at its published address or at the one with the revision's Web address.
  • A revision without an address yet, for example below a page that is not published in that language, cannot be previewed. The admin then stays on the editor: "This revision has no address on the website yet, so it cannot be previewed there."

The layout gets .Preview and .Revision, with the revision's Number, whether it is the Published one and PublishedURL, the same address without the preview. A banner tells editors what they see:

{{with .Revision}}
    <p class="preview-bar" role="status">
        {{tl localizer "Preview of revision %d" .Number}}{{if not .Published}} ({{tl localizer "not published"}}){{end}}.
        <a href="{{.PublishedURL}}">{{tl localizer "Show the published version"}}</a>
    </p>
{{end}}

Previews are sent with X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow and Cache-Control: private, no-store, without an ETag, so search engines leave them out and no cache keeps them.

A simple published flag

The other content modules, such as gallery, lists, people and documents, keep one version of each item with a published flag:

  • Publish and Unpublish switch the flag. Publishing needs a complete translation in the default language. Unpublish asks "Take this off the website?" first.
  • Save changes the item at once, also on the live site when it is published, and the admin says "Changes saved.".
  • New items start unpublished, at the end of the list. The ↑ and ↓ buttons in the overview set the order; they are hidden while the list is searched.

There is no history, preview or schedule for these items. The Editing section of each module's README says how its content is published.

Scheduled publishing

Revisioned content can be published and taken offline at a planned time. Open the revision to publish, unfold Schedule this revision in the publication box and fill in one or both fields:

  • Publish at publishes the selected revision.
  • Unpublish at takes the item offline. It must come after Publish at.

The times are in the site's timezone (Site settings › Timezone), shown next to the fields, and stored in UTC. The box then shows the plan, and Cancel schedule removes it. A time in the past is carried out on the next check. A time that cannot be read, or an Unpublish at that does not come after Publish at, is refused with "Choose when to publish or unpublish; unpublishing must come after publishing."

Publishing or unpublishing by hand cancels the plan: the editor decided now, and the plan would undo it. The admin asks for confirmation first, "Publishing now cancels the schedule. Continue?" or "Unpublishing now cancels the schedule. Continue?", and says afterwards that the schedule was cancelled.

The app checks for due changes every Config.ScheduleInterval, 30 seconds by default:

app := webthings.New(webthings.Config{
    ScheduleInterval: time.Minute,
})
  • A planned change has the same effects as the publish button; for a page, its address and the menu are updated too.
  • A change that can no longer be made, for example because the default language's translation is incomplete, is dropped and logged.
  • Several servers on one database can all run the check: each change is made by one of them.
  • A negative interval stops the background check; App.RunSchedules(ctx) runs it once, for example in tests or from a job of your own.
  • Permanent items, such as the home page, can be scheduled for publication, not for unpublication.

Modules with revisioned content take part through Parts.Scheduled; the plan is a content.Schedule (see content/schedule.go). The banners module has a window of its own instead: Show from and Show until.

Feeds

The pages of the publishing and events modules, such as news and an agenda, offer Atom and RSS feeds, which visitors follow in a feed reader: of the published posts, and of the published events that have not ended (see Publishing and Events). Publishing a post or event, by hand or at its planned time, puts it in the feeds of its page, and unpublishing it takes it out. Items in feeds, on the General card of Site settings, sets how many items each feed lists: 10, 20, 50 or 100, 20 by default. The site's code can give the feeds of one instance a size of their own instead (WithFeedSize), which the setting does not change.

Review before publishing

A site can ask for a reviewer's approval before revisioned content goes online. The review is off by default, and while it is off nothing changes.

Switching it on

The Review card in Site settings has a box for every section with revisions: Pages and each instance of the publishing and events modules. In a ticked section, only revisions that a reviewer approved are published. Only administrators can change the card; editors who may read Site settings see it read-only.

Reviewers need the Review right in the section's row of a group; see Accounts and permissions.

The states

State Meaning
Draft Nobody asked for a review. Every new revision starts here, so a changed text needs a new approval.
In review An editor submitted the revision for review.
Approved A reviewer approved it; it can be published.
Rejected A reviewer sent it back, with a note why.

The publication box shows the selected revision's state, who submitted and reviewed it and when, and the reviewer's note. The revision history shows the state of each revision.

Who does what

  • An editor with the edit right presses Submit for review on a draft or rejected revision. The published revision cannot be submitted.
  • A newer submission sends an older revision of the item that is still in review back to draft: the newest one is the one to review.
  • A reviewer opens the revision and, under Review this revision, presses Approve or Reject. Both take a note of at most 500 characters; a rejection needs one: "Write why the revision is rejected."
  • A reviewer who may also publish can tick Publish this revision now to approve and publish in one step.
  • Someone with both the edit and the review right can approve a revision they submitted. Administrators have every right.

Publishing needs an approval

  • Publish this revision shows only for an approved revision. Publishing any other revision is refused, also for editors with the publish right: "This revision needs a reviewer's approval before it can be published."
  • Scheduling a publication needs an approved revision too. Unpublishing needs no approval.
  • The scheduler checks again when the time comes. A plan made before the review was switched on, for a revision that is not approved, is dropped and logged.
  • When the site settings cannot be read, publishing waits for an approval rather than skipping it.

The dashboard and e-mail

  • Needs attention on the dashboard lists at most eight revisions that wait for your review, marked Waiting for review, the longest waiting first, with their section and who submitted them. It shows only sections where you have the review right.
  • The page tree and the overviews of posts and events show In review for an item whose newest revision waits for a reviewer.
  • When an editor submits a revision, everyone else with the review right in that section gets a short plain-text e-mail in the admin's language, with a link to the revision. It is only sent when the admin can send mail, as for the password reset link (see Accounts and permissions).

Security settings

The Security card in Site settings decides how the site's pages protect visitors. Only administrators can change it; editors who may read Site settings see it read-only.

  • Other sites may embed pages is whether other sites may show the site's pages in a frame: No, only this site, the default, Yes, any site or No, not even this site.
  • Content-Security-Policy is Off, the default, Report only, block nothing or Enforce. With a policy, browsers run only the scripts and styles the site serves itself, which blocks most code injected into a page. With Report only, block nothing, browsers block nothing and report what the policy would block, and the site writes it to its log. Check the log, then choose Enforce. A theme with styles or scripts written into its pages needs changes first.
  • Outside sources are other sites the pages may load from, one directive per line followed by addresses, such as frame-src https://www.youtube-nocookie.com for embedded videos. The directives are img-src, media-src, font-src, style-src, script-src, connect-src, frame-src, worker-src, manifest-src and form-action. The site's own files and its media storage are always allowed.

A line without one of these directives or without addresses, or with a source such as 'unsafe-inline', 'unsafe-eval' or *, is refused at the field with "Each line needs a directive, such as frame-src, and addresses, such as https://www.youtube-nocookie.com. Inline code, eval and every site (*) cannot be allowed.", and nothing is saved. The settings apply without a restart. See Security headers and A Content-Security-Policy of the site's own.

The server configuration can decide a setting instead of the card (see Configuration). With Config.ContentSecurityPolicy set, Content-Security-Policy shows that policy, disabled, with the note "Set by the server configuration." The Performance card does the same for The site keeps pages in memory for when Config.OutputCacheTTL is set, or when Config.Development or Config.ReloadTemplates turns the cache off: it shows the time that applies, or Off. Saving such a card keeps the stored setting of that field and saves the other fields.

The trash

Move to trash moves an item to the trash. The admin asks "Move this item to the trash?" first and says "Moved to the trash." afterwards.

  • The item leaves the website at once: its address, the menu, the site search and the sitemap. It also leaves the admin's lists, counts and dashboard.
  • Its web address, and any other value that must be unique, is free again for another item.
  • A planned publication change is cancelled. The item keeps its revisions, its publication and the media it uses.

Trash, under System in the admin navigation, lists the deleted items per section, with when and by whom each was deleted. The search field searches them, and a section's tab shows that section alone, 50 items per page. The Trash button on every overview, the page tree and Media included, opens the trash at that section.

Tick the items, or the box in the head of a section's table to tick all of that section's items on the page, and choose:

  • Restore selected brings them back as they were. A published item is on the website again.
  • Delete selected for good removes them with their revisions, after the question "Delete the selected items for good? This cannot be undone."

Both buttons stay disabled until an item is ticked. Without JavaScript they stay enabled and the boxes in the heads are not shown; a post without a ticked item is then refused with "Select at least one item.", and the trash stays as it was.

Restoring refuses an item that cannot come back and says why; the other selected items are still restored:

  • another item uses its web address now: "This item cannot be restored: another item uses its web address now.", for a page "Another page at this level already uses this web address, or the address is reserved.";
  • a page whose parent page is in the trash: restore the parent first;
  • a page whose module is placed on another page now.

Content in the trash still uses its media files, so the library cannot delete those files until that content is deleted for good. The trash is never emptied by itself: items stay until someone deletes them for good.

Seeing a section's trash needs the read right, restoring and deleting for good the delete right; see Accounts and permissions. Accounts and groups do not go to the trash.

Permanent items

A permanent item always stays on the website. Its editor says so in a box of its own, and has no Unpublish and no Move to trash; its schedule only has Publish at. Unpublishing, planning an unpublication and deleting are refused with the reason, also from a screen opened before the item became permanent. Saving, publishing a newer revision and planning a publication still work.

  • Administrators mark an item in its editor with Make permanent, and take the mark away with Remove permanent mark. Both ask for confirmation first. The administrator also needs the edit right in the section, which they have unless Config.Authorize says otherwise.
  • An item with a planned unpublication cannot be marked: "Cancel the planned unpublication first: a permanent item stays on the website."
  • Some items are permanent by their nature, such as the home page. Their mark cannot be removed. A module names its own with Permanent in the editor.Config of its section.

Links to a page

The admin knows which published content links to which page or item: the text of the published pages, and the published content of the modules that report their links, such as posts, events and the button of a banner (see Using modules). A link counts when it leads to an address on the site: a path such as /en/about, a relative link, which counts from the address of the text it is in, as a browser follows it (team in the text of /en/about leads to /en/team, about/team to /en/about/team), or a full address on the site's own host (Config.BaseURL). Links to other websites, e-mail and phone links and media files do not count, and neither do drafts.

The admin looks for the links when an editor or the report below needs them, never for visitors. It keeps what it found until something visitors see changes on the same server, and for Config.CacheTTL at most, 30 seconds by default, so changes made on other servers show within that time.

Before a page goes offline

The editor of a published page lists the published content that links to it or to an address below it, such as a page below it or a post on its module page: "2 published items link to this page.", with the title of each, linked to its editor, and its section and language, such as "News · en". Content below the page itself is left out, as it goes with the page. While such links exist, Unpublish asks "Published items link to this page. Unpublish it anyway?" instead of "Take this off the website?", and Move to trash asks "Published items link to this page. Move it to the trash anyway?".

With the redirects module, editors who may create redirects also get Unpublish and redirect. Choose a page under Redirect to, the parent page unless you choose another; the page itself and the pages below it are not offered. The page then goes offline, and its addresses redirect to the chosen page. So do the addresses of the published pages below it and the linked addresses below those, such as a post on a module page. Each address redirects to the chosen page in its own language, or in the site's default language when the chosen page has none in that language. The message afterwards says how many old addresses redirect now.

A new address

A revision with a new Web address or another parent page gives the page, and the pages below it, new addresses once it is published. The editor of a published page shows the change before that, per language, such as /en/about → /en/about-us, or "not on the website" where the page would not be on the site in that language. When content links to the old address, it says how many published items do: "2 published items link to the old address."

With the redirects module, Publish this revision comes with a box, Redirect the old addresses to the new ones, ticked by default. The old addresses of the page, of the pages below it and the linked addresses below those then redirect to their new addresses, so links and search engines that use an old address still arrive. Without the module, or without the right to create redirects, publishing asks first while content links to the old address: "Published items link to the old address, and their links will lead nowhere. Publish anyway?"

Links to an item

Posts, events, albums, people, directory entries and the categories of the publishing and directory modules have an address of their own, such as /en/news/hello or /en/news/category/tips. The editor of such an item, once it is published, lists the published content that links to its address in the same way: "1 published item links to this item.", with the title, section and language of each. While such links exist, Unpublish asks "Published items link to this item. Unpublish it anyway?", and Move to trash asks "Published items link to this item. Move it to the trash anyway?". With the redirects module, editors who may create redirects also get Unpublish and redirect. Under Redirect to, the page the item is shown on is chosen unless you choose another. The item then goes offline, and its address in each language redirects to the chosen page in that language, or in the site's default language when the chosen page has none in that language.

A revision of a post or an event with a new Web address gives the item a new address once it is published. The editor shows the change before that, per language, such as /en/news/hello → /en/news/hello-again, and how many published items link to the old address. With the redirects module, Publish this revision comes with the box Redirect the old addresses to the new ones, ticked by default, as for a page. Without the module, or without the right to create redirects, publishing asks first while content links to the old address.

Albums, people, directory entries and categories have no revisions: saving a published one with a new Web address changes its address at once. For editors who may create redirects, the old address then redirects to the new one on its own, and the message says so: "Changes saved. 1 old address redirects now." While content links to the item, its editor says so before you save: "Saving it with another address redirects the old address to the new one." Without the redirects module, or without the right, the old address leads nowhere.

The entries of a directory category have addresses below it, such as /en/directory/food/bakery. The category's editor counts the links to them apart, "1 published item links to an address below this item.", and asks before the category goes offline: "Published items link to addresses below this item. Unpublish it anyway?" Unpublish and redirect redirects the entries' addresses as well as the category's. Only the category's own address gets a redirect when its Web address changes; its entries' old addresses redirect to the new ones without one, as for an entry that moved to another category. The categories of the documents module have no editor of their own, so they have none of this.

Broken links

Broken links, above the page tree under Pages, lists the addresses on the site that links in published pages and module content lead to, where the website has no page. Each address shows the content that links there, linked to its editor, and the reason:

  • "The address does not start with a language of the website.";
  • "The page with this address is not published.", with a link to the page's editor;
  • "The page with this address is in the trash.", with a link to the trash;
  • "No page has this address."

A link to an address that a redirect leads from, to a page or to another website, is not broken. An address below a module page always counts as found, since the module answers there, so a link to a post that was taken off the site is not listed.

Fix the link in its content, publish the page again, or redirect the address. With the redirects module, choose a page under Redirect to next to the address and press Create redirect: the address then redirects to that page in the address's language, or in the site's default language when the page has none in that language. Without the module, the report says "With the Redirects module, you can redirect such an address to another page here."; with it, users without the right to create redirects read "You need the right to create redirects."

Seeing the report needs the read right in Pages. Redirects made here and in the editor of a page or an item need the create right in the redirects module's row; see Accounts and permissions.

The edit link on the site

Editors who are signed in to the admin see the public site like visitors do, plus a link to the admin screen of what they look at. The layout gets it as .Editor:

{{with .Editor}}
    <a class="edit-link" href="{{.EditURL}}">{{tl localizer "Edit"}}</a>
{{end}}

.Editor is a frontend.EditLink with the editor's Name and the EditURL. It is set only when the editor may edit there:

  • on a page, it opens that page in the admin;
  • on a module item, such as a post, it opens that item;
  • on other module screens, it opens the module's section.

The admin screen opens in the language of the page. Visitors, editors without the right to edit and the search and "not found" screens get no link.

Other links into the admin, such as one to the dashboard in the footer, use the template function adminURL. It gives signed-in editors the address and visitors "", so the admin's address stays off public pages:

{{with adminURL "admin.dashboard"}}<a href="{{.}}">{{tl localizer "Admin"}}</a>{{end}}

See Template functions.

The admin's session cookie reaches the public site for this. It is only checked when it is present, so visitors cost nothing. Pages for signed-in editors are sent with Cache-Control: private, no-store, so no cache keeps them or shows them to visitors, and the site renders them anew for every request. For visitors, the site keeps the pages it sent in memory for a while, as Site settings › Performance allows: 1 minute by default. A change made on the same server shows to them at once all the same, in the admin and when content is published at its planned time. A change made by another server of the site, and what changes with time alone, such as an event that has passed, can take that minute; see The output cache. Visitors' browsers and caches keep pages as Site settings › Performance allows too: by default they ask the site every time, so a published change shows at once; with a time set there, it can take that long, plus the refresh time when one is set. Middleware can tell editors apart with frontend.Editor(ctx); the stats module uses it to leave editors out of its counts. See frontend/editor.go.

The dashboard

The admin opens on a dashboard of what is going on. The page shows at once, with its buttons; its three lists load right after it, each on its own:

  • Needs attention lists the revisions that wait for your review (see Review before publishing) and the sections with a count, such as comments to approve.
  • Recently edited shows the items changed last, with who changed them and when, in the site's timezone.
  • Scheduled lists the planned publication changes, the soonest first, each marked Goes online or Goes offline.
  • Buttons create something new, such as a post or an event; with many sections they are collected in a menu.
  • View website opens the site.

A time on the day before, of or after today reads "Yesterday 09:30", "Today 14:05" or "Tomorrow 08:00", by the dates in the site's timezone, also on a day its clocks skip midnight; other times show their date, such as "5 Oct 2026 14:05".

Each list shows at most eight entries. A list waits at most five seconds for the sections. A section that fails or takes longer is left out, and the list names it below the others, for example "Could not load: News, Agenda". Reload the page to try again.

Each editor sees only the sections they may read, and the buttons only where they may create.

The breadcrumbs in the header of every admin page start at Dashboard, followed by the section and the page, such as Dashboard › News › Open studio; on the dashboard they show Dashboard alone. Pages for people who are not signed in, such as the sign-in page, have none.

Until the setup guide is finished, administrators see a card above the lists: "Finish setting up your site", with the steps done, such as "2 of 5 steps done", and Continue setup. Once every step is done or skipped, it reads "Everything is ready — finish setting up" and "All steps done", with Finish. Editors never see the card or the guide; see Set up the site.

Pages from the setup guide

The Pages step of the setup guide makes a site's first pages. It has a row for every module instance that can be on a page, and for three ordinary pages: About us, Contact and Privacy. Each row has a box, Create page, and a title in each language, filled in with the row's title; the boxes of the modules are ticked. Create the ticked pages makes each ticked page below Home:

  • a module's page is published at once, so visitors can reach the module;
  • an ordinary page is a draft, for you to write first.

A row that has a page already shows it, such as "On page News", and has no box, so posting the step again creates nothing twice. An ordinary page counts as there when a page below Home has its title in any language. A title that makes no address is refused at its row: "A page with this address exists already, or the title makes no address. Choose another title." Once there are pages, the step offers Write the first content, the dashboard's buttons that create something new.

Who else is on this page

The admin's header shows a round chip with the initials of every other person who has the same page open, in the same colour on every page. Pointing at a chip shows "Anna is also on this page". At most five chips show; more people show as one chip such as +3, which names them when you point at it. You never see yourself, also not with several tabs open.

  • The chips show names only, never e-mail addresses. An account without a name shows as "Another user", with ? as its initials.
  • Every page of a section you may read has the chips: its overview, an item's editor and its other screens. The dashboard, Your account, Trash and the forms for a new item have none.
  • All language tabs of an item are one page, and so are its older revisions: everyone in the item's editor counts.
  • People appear as soon as they open the page and disappear when they close it or go to another one. Someone who signs out disappears at once. A tab that ends without closing, for example on a laptop that goes to sleep, disappears within about a minute, and so does someone whose account is disabled.
  • A tab in the background still counts as present. After 30 seconds it stops following who comes and goes, and catches up when you return to it.

The chips lock nothing. Two people can still change the same item at the same time, and the later save wins for everything on its screen, such as the text of its language tab; the other languages stay as they were. With revisions, the earlier save stays in the Revision history and can be restored as a new draft. Content with a simple published flag keeps only the later save.

Counts and notes in the admin

Some sections show a count next to their name in the navigation when something waits for an editor: comments to approve in the comments module, new entries in the forms module and proposed news in the submissions module. The sections are asked at the same time, and a count that takes longer than a second is left out on that page, so a slow section never holds up the admin.

Overviews can show a muted note after an item's title, such as a download count in the documents module, and "Missing translation" for items that are not complete in the language of the tab.

Searching and messages

Lists in the admin, such as pages, media, accounts and each module's items, have a search field at the top. It searches while you type and finds the items that contain every word, ignoring case and accents. × or Escape clears it. An empty overview says "Nothing here yet." and, for editors who may create, offers the section's "New …" action where it has one, such as New post; a search without results says so instead.

Long lists are split into pages, usually of 50 items, with Previous and Next below them; the media library shows 48 files per page. A search starts again at the first page. Lists that are read from the database a page at a time, such as comments, form submissions and newsletter subscribers, search the first 5000 items of the tab only.

Messages after an action, such as "Changes saved.", appear at the bottom right, or across the bottom on a phone; only the sign-in and password reset pages show theirs on the page. A value the admin refuses, such as an e-mail address that is already in use or a password that is too short, is shown at its field. So is a value it cannot read, such as letters in a number field or a choice that is not in the list, and the form is not saved. A required field with only spaces counts as empty, with "This field is required.", and spaces around a value do not count toward a minimum length. Required choices, such as the default language, are marked like other required fields. A group of checkboxes, such as Languages in the site settings or a post's Categories, is a fieldset with the field's name as its legend, so screen readers announce the name with each box. Confirmations disappear after five seconds, but not while the pointer or the focus is on them; warnings and errors stay until they are closed.

A request the admin cannot carry out shows an error message the same way, and the page stays as it is: "The request failed. Please try again." after an error on the server (status 500), "You are not allowed to do this." without the right (403), "This request could not be read." for a post that no admin form sends (400), and "Upload request too large." for a post larger than the admin accepts (413). Without JavaScript, the browser shows the sentence alone.

Date and time fields, such as Publish at, show and read times in the site's timezone, as visitor forms on the site do. An event's Start and End are read as typed, in the event's own Timezone, and a new event starts at the next full hour there, also in a timezone that is a half or a quarter of an hour off, such as Asia/Kolkata. A start or end that cannot be read is refused at its field. Number fields take a decimal point, not a comma, such as a directory entry's Latitude and Longitude, which must lie between −90 and 90 and between −180 and 180.

Guides.Title: Accounts and permissions
Guides.Summary: Everyone who works in the admin signs in with an account of their own. Administrators may do everything; editors get the rights of their groups, section by section.
Guides.Body:
Administrators and editors

Every account has one of two roles:

Role May
Administrator do everything, including managing accounts and groups
Editor do what their groups allow; nothing else

An editor without groups sees only the dashboard and their own account under System. The dashboard shows only the sections an editor may read, and "New …" buttons only where they may create. Give editors rights through groups, and keep the administrator role for the people who manage the site.

The admin's header shows who else has the same page open; see Who else is on this page. It does so only on pages of sections the viewer may read, and only for others who may read them too. It shows names, never e-mail addresses.

The first administrator

On an empty database, the first start creates an administrator from Config.AdminEmail and Config.AdminPassword:

app := webthings.New(webthings.Config{
    AdminEmail:    os.Getenv("WEBTHINGS_ADMIN_EMAIL"),
    AdminPassword: os.Getenv("WEBTHINGS_ADMIN_PASSWORD"),
})

Once any account exists, both are ignored, so changing them later changes nothing. The password needs at least 12 characters; a shorter one stops the start with an error. The starter reads both from the environment and task run sets local defaults, as Getting started describes.

Without them, a start without accounts logs a one-time link to the setup screen, /admin/setup?token=…, on Config.BaseURL or else on the address the site listens on. /admin is the default admin path; Config.AdminPath can move the admin, and this guide's addresses with it. Every start makes a new link. That form creates the first administrator, signs them in and opens the setup guide (see Set up the site). Without the link's token, and once any account exists, the address answers 404. The sign-in page says to use the link from the server's log: "search the log for “no account exists yet”". While no account exists, opening the sign-in page also logs the link again, at level WARN and at most once a minute, so it is at the end of the log. You can also create the account in Go, after app.Start:

_, err := app.Auth.CreateUser(ctx, "anna@example.com", "Anna", password, auth.Admin)

To keep the password out of the code and the environment, app.InviteAdministrator(ctx, email) creates an administrator with a password nobody knows and returns a link to the admin's password reset page, where the account's owner chooses one. The link works for an hour (auth.ResetLifetime). It is on Config.BaseURL, or without one the path below the site's address, such as /admin/reset-password?token=…. It works once the app has started, also on a site with accounts; before Start it returns webthings.ErrNotStarted, for an address that is no address auth.ErrEmail, and for one that has an account auth.ErrDuplicate. Give the link only to the owner of the address: it opens the account. The starter's go run . admin you@example.com prints such a link.

Accounts

Accounts in the admin is for administrators only. It lists every account with badges for its role and status, and the search field finds one by e-mail address or name. Next to the list is the form for a new account: an e-mail address, an optional name, a password of at least 12 characters and a role.

Choosing an account shows a card with its name, role, status and when it was created; New account at the top brings back the form. Below the card, an administrator can:

  • change its e-mail address and name;
  • change its role;
  • choose its groups;
  • disable it, or enable it again. A disabled account cannot sign in, and disabling it ends its sessions;
  • see its sessions that have not expired, with when each was created, expires and was last used, and revoke one;
  • delete it, with its sessions and group memberships. This cannot be undone: accounts do not go to the trash. Nobody can delete their own account.

At least one active administrator must remain: the last one cannot be disabled, made an editor or deleted.

Passwords

A password is set when the account is created. After that, only the account's owner changes it:

  • Your account, in the admin navigation of every account, changes your own password. It asks for the current one first, and wrong guesses count towards the sign-in limit (see Sessions). Your other sessions are signed out.
  • Forgot your password? on the sign-in page mails a link to choose a new password. The link works once, within an hour; an account gets at most three links per hour, and the page answers the same for addresses without an account. Choosing the new password signs the account out everywhere.

The admin offers the reset only with Config.Mail and Config.BaseURL, so the link is sent and points to the site (see E-mail). With Config.Insecure, for local development, it is always offered; without a sender the link is written to the log.

Groups and the matrix

Groups is for administrators only. A group has a name and a matrix of rights: a row for every section of the admin, and a column for every action.

The rows are Pages, Media, Site settings and a section for every module instance in main.go, such as News or Agenda, under the same headings as in the admin navigation. The columns are the actions:

Action In Pages and module content
Read see the list, open items and preview them on the site
Create add a new item
Edit save changes, restore an older revision, change the order, submit a revision for review
Publish publish, unpublish and schedule
Delete move an item to the trash, restore it or delete it for good
Review approve or reject a revision submitted for review
Export download personal data as CSV, where a section offers it

The Review column has a box only in sections with revisions: Pages and each instance of the publishing and events modules. The right matters only where Site settings › Review asks for a review. There, publishing and scheduling need an approved revision, also with the publish right, and a reviewer who may publish can approve and publish in one step. See Review before publishing.

The Export column shows only when a section offers an export, and has a box only in those sections: each instance of the newsletter module (its subscribers) and of the registrations module (the registrations of a subject). An export holds personal data, so read is not enough: only editors with the export right see Export CSV. No group has it until an administrator ticks it.

In Media, read opens the library, create uploads, edit changes titles and alternative texts, and delete moves files to the trash, restores them or deletes them for good. Site settings uses read and edit, and its rights also cover Theme. Only administrators change its Review and Security cards, which decide who may publish without a review, which sites may show the pages in a frame, and the site's Content-Security-Policy with its outside sources (see Security settings); others see them read-only, and a save of theirs is refused with 403. Modules with screens of their own use the same actions; their READMEs say what needs which, for example archiving a form submission needs edit, and accepting a proposed news item needs publish.

Boxes in the headings select a whole column (one action in every section), a row (every action of a section), a heading's sections or, at the top left, the whole matrix. A box shows a dash when only part of what it covers is selected. The column headings stay in view while you scroll.

Every screen opens with read, so any other right in a row grants read as well: checking a box checks read in its row, clearing read clears the row, and saving adds read to every row with another right. Editors without publish do not see the publish buttons; they save drafts that someone else publishes.

With read alone, an editor sees an item's editor, a media file's texts, Site settings and the theme's settings read-only, with a note that they can view but not change them: their fields are disabled and there is no save button. Buttons that need another right are hidden, such as the upload form in Media without create, and Use this theme without edit in Site settings. A screen or a post without the right is refused with status 403 and "You are not allowed to do this.": an error message at the bottom right for a request from the admin's pages, the sentence alone for any other; see Searching and messages.

Add editors to a group on their account's page. An editor in several groups gets all of their rights together. Changes to a group apply from the editor's next request.

A typical setup for a news site:

Group Rights
Writers News: read, create, edit · Media: read, create · Pages: read
Editors-in-chief News: everything · Pages: read, create, edit, publish · Media: everything
