With News ticked under Site settings › Review, the writers submit their posts and the editors-in-chief, who have the review right in News, approve and publish them.

Sections without a row

Some sections are not in the matrix:

  • Accounts and Groups are for administrators only. A module can mark its own admin sections the same way with Section.AdminOnly.
  • A section that shares another section's rights has no row of its own. Theme uses Site settings, and a news instance's categories use the rights of the news instance. A module sets this with Section.Permission, the ID of the section whose rights apply. See The admin of a module.

The trash

Deleting moves an item to the trash, under System in the admin navigation. The trash follows the rows of the matrix:

  • Read in a section shows that section's deleted items, with who deleted them. Editors without read in any section with a trash do not see Trash.
  • Delete in a section restores its items and deletes them for good.

Accounts and groups do not go to the trash: deleting one cannot be undone. See The trash.

Links and redirects

The editor of a published page lists the content that links to it to everyone who may read Pages, and the editor of a published post, event, album, person or directory entry to everyone who may read its section. Pages › Broken links needs the read right in Pages. The redirects that the editors and the report offer, with the redirects module, need the create right in the module's row, Redirects:

  • Unpublish and redirect also needs publish in Pages, or in the item's section;
  • the box Redirect the old addresses to the new ones comes with Publish this revision, so it needs publish in Pages or in the section as well;
  • saving an album, a person or a directory entry with a new Web address redirects its old address for users who may save it, with edit in its section;
  • Create redirect in the report needs nothing more.

Without the create right, editors see none of them, and the report tells them "You need the right to create redirects." A post of theirs to Unpublish and redirect or Create redirect is refused with 403, and publishing a revision or saving an item with a new Web address makes no redirects for them. See Links to a page.

Replacing the rule

Config.Authorize replaces the built-in rule with your own; without it, the built-in rule applies:

app := webthings.New(webthings.Config{
    Authorize: func(ctx context.Context, user auth.User, permission admin.Permission) bool {
        if user.IsAdmin() {
            return true
        }

        // Editors may do everything except delete, in every section.
        return permission.Action != admin.Delete
    },
})

permission.Section is the section's ID (pages, media, site or a module key), and permission.Action one of read, create, edit, publish, delete, review and export (admin.View, admin.Create, admin.Edit, admin.Publish, admin.Delete, admin.Review, admin.Export).

The function is asked for every check, also for administrators and their Accounts and Groups screens, so let it allow administrators. The groups are then not used. It can keep those screens from administrators, but it never opens them to editors: sections for administrators only stay so, whatever it returns, and so do the Review and Security cards of Site settings and the permanent mark of an item. It also decides who sees the edit link and previews on the site, and who gets the e-mail about a revision to review.

The function must be safe for concurrent use: requests ask it at the same time, and so does work in the background, such as finding the reviewers to e-mail.

Sessions

Sign in at /admin/login with the e-mail address and password. A session lasts 12 hours from signing in, and Sign out ends it at once. Signing in again in the same browser ends that browser's previous session.

After 10 failed attempts for one e-mail address within 15 minutes, signing in with that address is blocked until those 15 minutes have passed. The message does not tell whether the account exists.

The session is kept in a cookie named wt_admin: HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax and, unless Config.Insecure is set, Secure, so it is only sent over HTTPS. Signing in over plain HTTP needs Insecure; the starter sets it for local development through WEBTHINGS_INSECURE_HTTP. Never set it in production.

Passwords are stored as Argon2id hashes, and sessions and reset links only as SHA-256 digests of their tokens. Expired sessions and reset links, and failed sign-ins whose 15 minutes are over, are removed when the app starts and every hour after.

Form posts to the admin from other websites are refused with 403 Forbidden and "This request came from another website and was refused." (Go's http.CrossOriginProtection). Browsers say where a post comes from, so the admin's forms need no token: they keep working after a restart and on every server of the site.

The admin's language

Config.AdminLanguage is the language of the admin, the same for every account:

app := webthings.New(webthings.Config{
    AdminLanguage: "nl",
})

English (en, the default) and Dutch (nl) are built in; texts without a translation show in English. A catalogue in StateDir/translations/, such as nl.po, changes the admin's texts or adds a language; see Languages. Mail to staff, such as the notification of a new comment, is written in the same language (see E-mail).

The admin's language is not the language of the content: editors write every site language in the tabs of each page and item. See Languages.

Edit links on the site

Editors who are signed in to the admin see the public site as visitors do, plus a link to the admin screen of what they look at. Put it in the layout:

{{with .Editor}}<a class="edit-link" href="{{.EditURL}}">{{tl localizer "Edit"}}</a>{{end}}

.Editor is set only for a signed-in account that may edit what the page shows: the edit right in the section of that page, post or other item. The link opens the screen in the page's language. .Editor.Name is the account's name, or its address without one.

The session cookie reaches the public site for this. It is only checked when it is present, so visitors cost nothing, and pages for editors are sent with Cache-Control: private, no-store, so caches never keep or share them and editors always see the latest version. Visitors may get a kept page for as long as Site settings › Performance allows. Middleware can recognise editors with frontend.Editor(ctx), for example to leave them out of statistics. See Editing and publishing.

Next steps

  • Editing and publishing covers drafts, revisions and scheduling.
  • Configuration lists every setting of webthings.Config.
  • Deployment covers HTTPS and running the site in production.

Guides.Title: Databases
Guides.Summary: go-webthings keeps everything in one SQL database: SQLite by default, or PostgreSQL or MySQL. It creates and updates its tables itself every time the site starts.
Guides.Body:
SQLite

Without any database settings, the site uses SQLite in its state folder:

var/site.sqlite

The file is created on first start. The default connection string is file:var/site.sqlite, with var replaced by Config.StateDir. go-webthings adds the settings it relies on to every SQLite DSN, including one you set yourself:

_foreign_keys=1&_busy_timeout=5000&_txlock=immediate&_time_format=sqlite&_timezone=UTC

A DSN that already sets one of them keeps its own value, so older connection strings keep working. Keep foreign keys on; the tables rely on them.

SQLite allows one writer at a time, so go-webthings keeps a single connection to it per process. That suits a site on one server. For several servers, use PostgreSQL or MySQL.

The SQLite driver is pure Go (modernc.org/sqlite), so building the site needs no cgo or C compiler; see Deployment. Driver is sqlite; sqlite3 is accepted too.

PostgreSQL

Set Driver to pgx and DSN to a connection URL or a key/value string:

webthings.Config{
    Driver: "pgx",
    DSN:    "postgres://website:secret@127.0.0.1:5432/website?sslmode=disable",
}

With the starter, set the environment instead:

WEBTHINGS_DB_DRIVER=pgx \
WEBTHINGS_DB_DSN='postgres://website:secret@127.0.0.1:5432/website?sslmode=disable' \
./bin/website

Create the database first and let the site's user own it, so it may create tables:

createuser --pwprompt website
createdb --owner website website

IDs are stored in native uuid columns.

MySQL

Set Driver to mysql and DSN to a go-sql-driver DSN:

webthings.Config{
    Driver: "mysql",
    DSN:    "website:secret@tcp(127.0.0.1:3306)/website",
}

go-webthings adds parseTime=true and clientFoundRows=true to the DSN when they are missing; it needs both. Create the database with the utf8mb4 character set, the default since MySQL 8.0:

CREATE DATABASE website CHARACTER SET utf8mb4;

MySQL commits table changes immediately, even inside a transaction. If a schema file fails halfway, part of it may already be applied; fix the cause and check the tables before starting again.

go-webthings' own tests run against PostgreSQL 18 and MySQL 8.4.

Tables and schema versions

Every core part and every module type keeps its tables in schema files. At start, go-webthings applies them in order: auth, media, site, pages, admin and frontend, then the modules in the order of app.Use. All tables start with wt_. The frontend part holds wt_kept_form, where visitors' posts with mistakes wait for their page; see Visitor forms.

The table wt_schema records the version each owner has reached:

owner version
auth 20261004000000
pages 20261004000000
module:publishing 20261004000000

Instances of one module type share its tables, so news and blog both live in the publishing tables, apart by their key. A module type's schema is applied when at least one of its instances is in app.Use. Removing an instance from main.go keeps its tables and its content.

Schema files

Schema files sit in one folder and are named <datetime>[_description].<flavour>.sql:

schema/20261004000000_init.sqlite.sql
schema/20261004000000_init.postgres.sql
schema/20261004000000_init.mysql.sql
schema/20261120093000_add_avatar.sqlite.sql
schema/20261120093000_add_avatar.postgres.sql
schema/20261120093000_add_avatar.mysql.sql
  • The datetime, YYYYMMDDHHMMSS, is the version.
  • The flavours are sqlite, postgres and mysql. Every version must exist in every flavour, even on a site that only uses one database; otherwise the start fails with "schema versions … differ …; add the missing files".
  • Only the files of the site's own database run, oldest first, and only those newer than the version in wt_schema.
  • Each file runs in a transaction and moves the version forward.
  • A statement ends with a semicolon at the end of a line. Lines starting with -- are skipped.

To change a table, add new files with a later datetime. Never change a file that a database has already applied: it will not run again.

A module passes its folder as Module.Schema, usually embedded in the binary:

//go:embed schema/*.sql
var schemaFiles embed.FS

func schema() fs.FS {
    files, _ := fs.Sub(schemaFiles, "schema")

    return files
}

See Writing a module.

Until go-webthings has its first release, its own schemas only have _init files, and those may still change. Nothing updates an existing database when an _init file changes: wt_schema already records its version, so it does not run again, and queries then fail on missing columns, such as created_by, or review_state in the _revision tables, which the review workflow added. After updating go-webthings, recreate a development database: stop the site, delete var/site.sqlite and start again. On PostgreSQL or MySQL, drop the database and create it again.

Audit columns

Tables of things people change record who changed them and when:

Columns
created_at, created_by When the row was made, and by whom.
updated_at, updated_by Its last change.
deleted_at, deleted_by When it went to the trash, and by whom; NULL while it is live.

The *_by columns hold a user ID, or NULL for visitors and the system, such as the scheduler. They have no foreign key, so the record stays when an account is deleted. Content, such as pages, media and the records of modules, has all six columns; tables whose rows cannot go to the trash, such as accounts, leave out deleted_at and deleted_by. Settings tables only have updated_at and updated_by. Logs, counters, join tables and the _translation tables have none. A _revision table has only created_at: a revision records its own author, and who submitted and reviewed it.

The user comes from the context. The admin puts the signed-in user there for every request (auth.WithUser calls db.WithActor), and db.Actor(ctx) returns it as a db.Ref, which is stored as NULL when empty. The content stores fill the columns themselves. Code that writes tables of its own takes the values from db.Stamp(ctx): the current time in UTC, cut to the microsecond that every database keeps, and db.Actor(ctx). Take one stamp per change and write it to every row the change touches. db.Affected checks a statement meant for a row that must exist: it returns db.ErrNotFound when no row matched, such as a member in the trash.

at, by := db.Stamp(ctx)

err := db.Affected(database.Exec(ctx, `
    UPDATE site_member
    SET email=?, updated_at=?, updated_by=?
    WHERE id=? AND deleted_at IS NULL`,
    email, at, by, id,
))

db.SoftTable writes the statements of a table whose rows go to the trash, limited to a part of the table with Scope, such as one instance. Delete fills deleted_at and deleted_by, Undelete empties them and fills updated_at and updated_by, Purge removes a row in the trash for good, and Trashed reads one page of the trash, the most recently deleted first, with how many rows it holds. Each returns db.ErrNotFound for a row that is not where it should be, and joins a transaction in the context:

members := db.SoftTable{DB: database, Table: "site_member", Scope: "instance=?", Args: []any{key}}

err := members.Delete(ctx, id)

Code outside the admin, such as an import, can set a user with db.WithActor(ctx, userID); without one, the columns stay NULL. db.Ref is the type for any ID column that may be NULL, in structs and as an argument: it also reads NULL as empty.

A unique index must leave deleted rows out, or a row in the trash keeps others from using its value. SQLite and PostgreSQL use a partial index. MySQL has no partial indexes, so it indexes a generated column that is NULL for deleted rows; a unique index allows many NULLs:

-- SQLite and PostgreSQL
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX site_member_email ON site_member (instance, email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

-- MySQL, inside CREATE TABLE site_member (...)
    live_email VARCHAR(254) AS (CASE WHEN deleted_at IS NULL THEN email END) STORED,
    UNIQUE INDEX site_member_email (instance, live_email)

Restoring a row whose value a live row took meanwhile then fails with a unique error, which db.IsUnique recognises. The subscribers of ../modules/newsletter/schema and the slugs of ../modules/people/schema work this way. SoftTable.Undelete(ctx, id, checks...) runs its checks first, in one transaction with the change, so a store can refuse with an error of its own instead, such as for a redirect whose old path another redirect uses now. See The admin of a module for the trash.

JSON columns

A value such as a list of form fields, type Fields []Field, can live in one text column as JSON. Its type stores and reads itself with db.JSONValue and db.ScanJSON:

// Value stores the fields as JSON.
func (f Fields) Value() (driver.Value, error) {
    return db.JSONValue(f)
}

// Scan reads fields stored by Value.
func (f *Fields) Scan(src any) error {
    return db.ScanJSON(src, f)
}

Use a TEXT column, or MEDIUMTEXT on MySQL for long values. NULL and empty text read as the zero value.

Backups

Back up the database and the uploads together.

  • SQLite: the state folder holds both. Copy the database with the sqlite3 tool, which is safe while the site runs, and the media/ folder:

    sqlite3 var/site.sqlite ".backup 'backup/site.sqlite'"
cp -R var/media backup/

    Or stop the site and copy the whole state folder.

  • PostgreSQL: pg_dump website > backup/website.sql, plus the media/ folder.

  • MySQL: mysqldump --single-transaction website > backup/website.sql, plus the media/ folder.

With Config.Storage set, uploads live in that storage instead of media/; back them up there. Keys such as the one that signs image URLs are stored in the database, so a restored site keeps its links working.

To restore, stop the site, put the database and the uploads back, and start it.

Switching databases

go-webthings does not copy content from one database to another. A site started on a new database is a new site: it gets a new home page, settings from the configuration and an administrator from AdminEmail and AdminPassword, or from the setup screen.

Choose the production database before editors start working. To move an existing site, copy the data yourself.

Testing

Two packages help in tests; use them in _test.go files only.

db/dbtest runs a test once per database, each with a fresh, empty database. SQLite always runs. Set WT_TEST_POSTGRES and WT_TEST_MYSQL to a server DSN to run on PostgreSQL and MySQL too; the user must be allowed to create databases, because each test creates one and drops it afterwards.

func TestShop(t *testing.T) {
    dbtest.Each(t, func(t *testing.T, database *db.DB) {
        ctx := context.Background()

        if err := database.ApplySchema(ctx, "module:shop", schema()); err != nil {
            t.Fatal(err)
        }

        // Test against database.
    })
}

dbtest.ForeignKeyError returns a real foreign key error from SQLite, for testing code that turns such errors into messages.

sitetest starts a complete site on SQLite in a temporary folder, signed in as an administrator, and drives it like a browser. Sent e-mail is kept in site.Mail; site.Mails(n) waits until n messages were sent, for mail sent in the background. sitetest.HasToast(body, level, text) tells whether an admin page shows a message, with level success, info, warn or error. The admin dashboard loads its panels after the page: site.Dashboard() returns it with the panels loaded, and site.Fragment(path, id) returns the part of a page with that ID, as HTMX asks for it. site.Request(req) sends a request of your own with the browser's cookies, such as one for a stream, and returns the response unread. site.App.AdminURL(name, args...) builds an admin address from a route name, wherever Config.AdminPath puts the admin. site.Mount and site.MountIn place a module on a published page, in one language or several, and return the page's editor; site.DraftPage gives a page an unpublished title and slug. sitetest.PNG(t, width, height) makes an image and site.Upload(name, data) adds it to the media library, and site.PostFiles(formPage, action, values, files...) sends a form with a file input, such as an import. See Caching and testing a module.

func TestNews(t *testing.T) {
    site := sitetest.Start(t, publishing.Module("news", "News"))

    site.Expect(site.App.AdminURL("admin.news.index"), http.StatusOK)
    site.Expect("/en/", http.StatusOK)
}

sitetest.StartWith takes options for other templates and configuration changes, StartingPoints to test the templates App.WriteTemplates generates, NoAccount for a fresh site that offers the setup screen, and OutputCache to keep the output cache on, which sites in tests have off. Its address is site.App.AdminURL("admin.setup", url.Values{"token": {site.App.SetupToken()}}), and a post to it needs the same token in the Token field.

Guides.Title: Deployment
Guides.Summary: A go-webthings site runs as one binary with its templates, its translations and a folder for its state. This guide covers building it, running it behind a reverse proxy and the settings that matter in production.
Guides.Body:
Build the binary

task build

runs CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -tags nodynamic -o bin/website . and writes the binary to bin/website. On Linux it is fully static, so it also runs on Alpine and in a scratch image. The demo's task build does the same and writes bin/demo.

go-webthings is pure Go, including its SQLite driver, so no build needs cgo or a C compiler. Cross-compiling works too, for example on a Mac for a Linux server:

GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -tags nodynamic -o bin/website .

Keep -tags nodynamic in your own build scripts and Dockerfiles. Without it, the Linux binary loads the system's C library when it starts, because the WebP package can use a libwebp installed on the system. It then runs on glibc systems such as Debian and Ubuntu, but not on Alpine or scratch. With the tag, it always uses its built-in WebP code.

Editors choose the site's timezone under Site settings, which needs the time zone database. Most Linux servers have it (the tzdata package). For a minimal system or container, embed it in the binary:

CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -tags nodynamic,timetzdata -o bin/website .

What the server needs

The starter reads its templates and translations from folders relative to the working directory, and keeps its state in WEBTHINGS_STATE_DIR:

/srv/website/
  bin/website        the binary
  templates/         the themes
  translations/      the site's .po files
/var/lib/website/    the state folder, writable by the site
  site.sqlite        the database, when the site uses SQLite
  media/             uploads and resized images, unless Storage is set
  translations/      optional: catalogues that change the admin's texts

When the state folder does not exist, the site creates it, accessible to its own user only. The admin, its assets and texts, the schema files and the modules' default templates are inside the binary. The admin only reads translations/, when you add it; see Languages.

Templates can be embedded too, since Config.Templates is any fs.FS:

//go:embed templates
var files embed.FS

templates, err := fs.Sub(files, "templates")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

// in the Config:
Templates: templates,

frontend.Translations reads a folder on disk, so translations/ stays in the working directory.

When the site sends mail over TLS or keeps media in S3 over HTTPS, the server also needs the usual CA certificates.

Settings for production

  • WEBTHINGS_LISTEN: the address to serve on. Keep 127.0.0.1:8092 behind a proxy on the same machine; use :8092 in a container.
  • BaseURL: the public address, such as https://example.com. It makes the addresses in sitemap.xml, robots.txt, share links, feeds and e-mail, and the IDs of feed entries, independent of the request's Host header. The admin's password reset needs it, and the start logs a warning without it.
  • TrustedProxies: the address of the reverse proxy, so visitors are known by their own address and links use the scheme and host the proxy reports.
  • Insecure: never set it in production. The admin's session cookie must stay HTTPS-only.
  • Development: never set it in production either. It shows anyone the details of a failing template; see Development mode. In the starter, leave WEBTHINGS_DEVELOPMENT unset. Without it, the start logs the problems of the templates at WARN, as template problem, and fails only when every page of the active theme would fail; read the log after a deploy (see Checking the templates at start).
  • Mail: without it, e-mail is only written to the log and the admin offers no password reset. The setup guide's E-mail step shows how the site sends and sends a test e-mail; see Mail and storage.
  • WEBTHINGS_ADMIN_EMAIL and WEBTHINGS_ADMIN_PASSWORD: used on the first start only. Remove them from the environment afterwards. Without them, the first start logs a one-time link, <AdminPath>/setup?token=… on BaseURL or else on the address the site listens on, where you create the first administrator. <AdminPath> is /admin unless Config.AdminPath says otherwise. Every start makes a new link until an account exists. While no account exists, opening <AdminPath>/login logs the link again, at level WARN and at most once a minute; search the log for "no account exists yet". To keep passwords out of the environment altogether, the starter's admin command, such as bin/website admin you@example.com with the site's environment, creates an administrator with App.InviteAdministrator and prints a link, valid for one hour, where its owner chooses the password. InviteAdministrator returns the link on BaseURL, or only its path without one, which the starter puts on the address it listens on. See Accounts and permissions.

The starter reads these from its environment, for example:

WEBTHINGS_BASE_URL=https://example.com
WEBTHINGS_TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.1
WEBTHINGS_SMTP_HOST=smtp.example.com
WEBTHINGS_SMTP_USERNAME=website
WEBTHINGS_SMTP_PASSWORD=secret
WEBTHINGS_SMTP_FROM='Example <hello@example.com>'

Configuration describes every field.

Behind a reverse proxy

go-webthings serves plain HTTP. Put a reverse proxy in front for HTTPS; the browser talks HTTPS to the proxy, so the secure session cookie works without Insecure.

The proxy should:

  • pass the original Host header, which the site uses for addresses when BaseURL is empty and to reject form posts from other sites;
  • add the visitor's address in X-Forwarded-For and the scheme in X-Forwarded-Proto, and be listed in TrustedProxies. Without that, every visitor has the proxy's address: limits on visitors' form posts and searches then apply to all visitors together, and statistics cannot tell visitors apart. With BaseURL empty, links then also start with http://. A standard Forwarded header (RFC 7239) works too: its for= names the visitor when there is no X-Forwarded-For or X-Real-IP, and its proto= and host= give the scheme and host when there is no X-Forwarded-Proto or X-Forwarded-Host;
  • accept request bodies of at least 10 MB, the largest upload the media library takes;
  • pass the admin's event stream on as it comes. While an admin page is visible, the browser keeps a stream of server-sent events open at <AdminPath>/presence, such as /admin/presence, for who else is on the page, with a heartbeat every 15 seconds. The site sends it with X-Accel-Buffering: no, which turns off nginx's buffering for it unless proxy_ignore_headers lists that header, and Caddy passes event streams on at once. A proxy timeout longer than 15 seconds, such as nginx's default of 60, keeps the stream open.

Caddy does all of this by default, including the certificate:

example.com {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8092
}

With nginx:

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name example.com;
    # ssl_certificate and ssl_certificate_key

    client_max_body_size 12m;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8092;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}

In both cases TrustedProxies is []string{"127.0.0.1"}. Neither needs to add security headers: the site sends them itself; see Security headers.

ListenAndServe limits a request to 30 seconds for reading, including an upload, and 60 seconds for the answer; the admin's event stream has no such limit. A proxy that buffers request bodies, as nginx does by default, keeps slow uploads within that.

The app is also an http.Handler. To serve HTTPS without a proxy, call Start, use the app as the Handler of your own http.Server and call Close once the server has shut down. Give Shutdown a deadline, as ListenAndServe does: the admin's event streams stay open until Close, so Shutdown would otherwise wait for them.

To serve on a listener you opened yourself, such as one systemd hands over with socket activation, call app.Serve(ctx, listener). It works like ListenAndServe, shutdown included, and logs the address it really listens on.

Security headers

The site sends its own security headers, so a proxy need not add them. Once the app has started, every response carries these two: those of the site and the admin, the redirects the router gives itself, such as from //en/ to /en/, and the answers of /healthz, /readyz and /metrics:

  • X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, so browsers never take a file, such as an upload, for another type than it has;
  • Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, so other sites learn only the site's address when visitors follow a link there.

Whether other sites may show the site's pages in a frame, such as an iframe, is the setting Other sites may embed pages on the Security card under Site settings, site.Settings.Framing. Only administrators can change the card; editors who may read Site settings see it read-only, and a post of theirs to it is refused with 403. Pages, module pages, the 404 page and the answers of visitor actions at /_/<key>/ get its headers:

Setting Framing Headers
No, only this site, the default same-origin X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN and Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'
Yes, any site any none
No, not even this site none X-Frame-Options: DENY and Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'

Older browsers follow X-Frame-Options, newer ones the frame-ancestors of the policy. With the default, other sites cannot lay a page over their own to trick visitors into clicking. The setting applies without a restart; other servers on the same database follow within CacheTTL. When the settings cannot be read, pages get the headers of same-origin. Settings.FramingPolicy() returns the value in effect, same-origin for an empty Framing; saving any other value fails with site.ErrInvalid.

Files at /media/, /assets/ and /theme/, sitemap.xml and robots.txt get no framing headers. Admin pages always send X-Frame-Options: DENY and Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none', whatever the setting. Uploads that Config.Storage serves from an address of its own, such as an S3 bucket's, do not pass the site, so their headers are that service's.

A Content-Security-Policy of the site's own

Core can send a strict Content-Security-Policy itself. It lets browsers run only the scripts and styles the site serves, so most code injected into a page does not run. It is off until an administrator changes Content-Security-Policy on the Security card under Site settings, site.Settings.ContentSecurity, or the site sets Config.ContentSecurityPolicy, which wins over the setting (see Configuration). The card is for administrators only, as above, and the setting applies without a restart. While Config.ContentSecurityPolicy sets the mode, the card shows that mode with the control turned off and the note "Set by the server configuration."

Setting Value Headers
Off, the default off only the frame-ancestors of the framing setting, as above
Report only, block nothing report-only the policy in Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only, and the frame-ancestors of the framing setting in Content-Security-Policy
Enforce enforce the policy in Content-Security-Policy, with the frame-ancestors of the framing setting

With report-only, browsers block nothing and report what the policy would block. They ignore frame-ancestors in a reported policy, so that directive stays enforced. Pages, module pages, the 404 page, the answers of visitor actions at /_/<key>/ and the admin get the policy; other responses, such as files at /media/, /assets/ and /theme/, sitemap.xml, robots.txt, the content API and /healthz, get none. When the settings cannot be read, the policy is off, unless Config.ContentSecurityPolicy sets it.

The policy is go-router's middleware.StrictCSP, with no 'unsafe-inline' and no 'unsafe-eval', which core completes for each page. The demo's home page with Enforce and the framing setting at its default gets:

Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'sha256-ikhAzHpIhdk6wxu+v3TtAkGM69wDavllgwgrXyKsTBc='; style-src 'self' 'sha256-5WNh79OqlbaM4rZ/DlkOnop5aYED/JCWp9ChTZ5ZOSQ='; img-src 'self' data:; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'; report-uri /_/csp-report; frame-ancestors 'self'
  • script-src has the hash of the page's import map, which {{importmap}} writes inline (go-importmap's ScriptHash()). The hash changes whenever a file in the map does; with ReloadTemplates it is that of the map the page writes.
  • style-src has the hash of the <style> element of go-partial's built-in error page (errors.StyleHash() of ext/errors). A theme without 500.gohtml shows that page, development mode shows it with the error, and the interactions client writes it into a page with reloadOnError. With Config.Development, style-src also has the hash of the {{debug}} box (debug.StyleHash()).
  • When the media storage serves its files from an address of its own, an absolute http or https address such as an S3 bucket's public URL, that origin is added to img-src and media-src, such as img-src 'self' data: https://media.example.com; see Storage.
  • The sources of Config.ContentSecuritySources, of Outside sources on the Security card and of the theme's "csp" in theme.json (see Themes) are added to their directives. A directive the policy does not have starts from default-src, so frame-src https://www.youtube-nocookie.com becomes frame-src 'self' https://www.youtube-nocookie.com.
  • report-uri is where browsers report what the policy blocks; see below.
  • frame-ancestors comes from the framing setting. With Yes, any site the policy has none.

The policy allows inline code by its hash, never by a nonce, so the output cache keeps a page with its policy, and a page it sends again carries the hashes it was rendered with. After a save of the card, the cache renders its pages again, with the new policy.

Outside sources takes one directive per line, followed by its sources, such as frame-src https://www.youtube-nocookie.com https://player.vimeo.com for embedded videos. site.CheckCSPSources checks each line, and also Config.ContentSecuritySources at Start and a theme's "csp":

  • The directive is one of connect-src, font-src, form-action, frame-src, img-src, manifest-src, media-src, script-src, style-src and worker-src.
  • A source is an address with the scheme http, https, ws or wss, such as https://*.example.com/embed/; 'self'; one of the schemes https:, wss:, data: and blob:, but not in script-src; or a hash such as 'sha256-…', in script-src and style-src only.

Anything else is refused, such as 'unsafe-inline', 'unsafe-eval', *, a nonce, 'strict-dynamic' or a line without sources. The card then shows "Each line needs a directive, such as frame-src, and addresses, such as https://www.youtube-nocookie.com. Inline code, eval and every site (*) cannot be allowed." at the field, with status 422, and saves nothing. Start fails with an error that wraps site.ErrCSPSource, also for a theme's "csp". It also fails, with an error of its own, for a Config.ContentSecurityPolicy that is not empty, off, report-only or enforce. In Go, Settings.ContentSecurityPolicy() returns the setting in effect, site.CSPOff, site.CSPReportOnly or site.CSPEnforce, and off for an empty one; saving another value fails with site.ErrInvalid. Settings.ContentSecuritySources holds the outside sources as text, which site.ParseCSPSources reads by directive.

Browsers report what the policy blocks, or would block with report-only, to /_/csp-report (the route csp.report), in the format of report-uri or of the Reporting API. Each violation is logged at level Warn as content security policy violation, with the disposition, the directive, the blocked address, the page and the file the violation is in, these three without their query, the line, the column and the first 80 characters of the sample. Nothing is stored. Each visitor may send 30 reports a minute and gets 429 for more, at most 60 are logged a minute in all, and reports about browser extensions are left out. To switch the policy on, choose Report only, block nothing, use the site and the admin, read the log, change what it names, then choose Enforce.

With report-only or enforce, the admin gets the site's policy with the hash of its own import map (Admin.ImportMapHash()) instead of the site's, and frame-ancestors 'none', which stays enforced with report-only. Its pages have no style attribute, <style> element, inline script or event handler attribute, so the admin works under the policy. A theme's preview in the admin is a page of the site: its policy has the hashes of both import maps and the theme's sources. With the policy off, the preview sends only the admin's frame-ancestors 'none', like every admin page.

What the policy means for the site's templates:

  • The pages of the starting points (App.WriteTemplates(dir, "site")) and the modules' default templates have no <style> element, no style attribute, no inline script and no event handler attribute. The spam trap of visitor forms has the class form-honeypot instead of a style attribute, and webthings.css hides it; see The hidden fields. The bars of a poll's results are <meter> elements.
  • {{structuredData}} writes a <script type="application/ld+json">. Browsers do not run such a data block, so script-src does not block it.
  • A colour or select setting with "css" in theme.json reaches the page as a custom property of /theme/<theme>/values.css, linked by {{styles}} or {{themeStyle}}, and a focal point as a class from {{focalClass}}, whose rule is in /_/focal-points.css, linked by {{styles … "focal-points.css"}} or {{assetStyle "focal-points.css"}}: neither is blocked. A theme's own style attributes, <style> elements, inline scripts and event handler attributes, such as a style attribute with {{objectPosition}}, are blocked with Enforce and reported with report-only; see Themes. A setting with fixed options, written as a data attribute that the theme's stylesheet reads, is not.
  • go-partial's error box, which takes the place of a part of a page that failed, such as the answer to a failing HTMX request in development mode, has classes and no inline style. go-partial's partial-errors.css styles it, which core serves at /_/partial-errors.css; {{styles}} in the layout links it first, and a layout without {{styles}} links it with {{assetStyle "partial-errors.css"}}.

A site may also send a policy of its own from the proxy in front of it, as a header of its own. A browser enforces every policy it gets, so a page must pass both. A handler around the app may set the header before the app answers instead. With the setting off, core merges the framing setting's frame-ancestors into that policy on pages, the 404 page and the answers of visitor actions, directive by directive: the policy keeps its other directives, and a frame-ancestors of its own gives way to the setting's, unless the setting is Yes, any site. The admin merges frame-ancestors 'none' into it the same way. With enforce, the handler's policy stays as well: the site's policy replaces only the directives it names, so others, such as upgrade-insecure-requests, stay, and a directive both name, such as a script-src with 'unsafe-inline', becomes the site's strict one, so it cannot weaken it; frame-ancestors follows the framing setting. With report-only, the handler's policy stays enforced, with the framing setting's frame-ancestors, and the policy reported is the handler's with the site's directives applied, without frame-ancestors. Any further policy, a second header, stays as it is. This holds for pages, the 404 page, the answers of visitor actions and the admin. Other responses, such as files at /assets/ and /theme/, keep the handler's policy as it is. The output cache keeps pages with their headers, so a page it keeps can be sent with the policy it was rendered with: keep the handler's policy the same while the site runs.

Caching and compression

The Performance card under Site settings in the admin decides how pages reach visitors. Its settings apply without a restart; other servers on the same database follow within CacheTTL. Its output cache, which keeps pages in each server's memory, has a section of its own: The output cache.

Compress responses is on by default. Browsers that accept gzip get compressed responses of 1 KiB or more, on the whole site and in the admin: pages, stylesheets, scripts, JSON, XML and SVG. Other images, video, WOFF fonts and event streams are sent as they are, and so are HEAD requests, requests for a range and responses that are encoded already. Responses that could be compressed say Vary: Accept-Encoding, so caches keep both versions apart. Turn the setting off when the proxy compresses instead.

Browsers and caches keep pages for sets how long pages for visitors may be kept without asking the site. The default is no time: pages are sent with Cache-Control: no-cache, so browsers and caches ask every time. With a time, pages are sent with Cache-Control: public, max-age=…, and Then show the kept page while refreshing adds stale-while-revalidate=…. Changes then show after at most that time. An address with a query, such as a search or a form's result, is always sent with no-cache.

Every page for visitors also gets a weak ETag, a hash of the page, the same whether the page is sent compressed or not. A browser or cache that asks again with If-None-Match gets 304 Not Modified without the page when it has not changed, so asking every time costs little. This applies to complete HTML pages and to the Atom and RSS feeds of modules with status 200, for GET and HEAD; a page whose module sets a Cache-Control of its own keeps that one. Left as they are:

  • pages for signed-in editors, which are sent with Cache-Control: private, no-store;
  • responses that are private or no-store, set a cookie, have an ETag of their own or are streamed;
  • other statuses, such as the 404 page;
  • files at /media/, /theme/ and /assets/, which keep their own headers.

Feeds, such as a news page's feed.atom and feed.rss, get the same Cache-Control as pages, and also say when they last changed, in Last-Modified. That time never goes back: it is when the server first sent the feed as it is now, or the time the feed gives itself, such as that of its newest entry, when that is later, so taking a post off the site moves it forward too. A reader that asks with If-Modified-Since alone gets 304 Not Modified while the feed has not changed, and the whole feed after a change; one that sends the ETag in If-None-Match is answered by the ETag. This holds for feeds the output cache keeps and for those it leaves alone. Each server keeps these times in its own memory, so after a restart, or from another server, a reader that asks by the time gets the whole feed once more. A time the server's clock has not reached yet is not sent, such as that of a feed that changed twice within one second. Pages send no Last-Modified, so they are checked by their ETag alone.

Pages also say Vary for the HTMX request headers, since an HTMX request may get only part of a page. A CDN that keeps pages should pass requests with the admin's session cookie, wt_admin, to the site, so editors see the latest pages and their edit links. It should pass requests with a wt_form_<key> cookie too: that cookie brings a visitor's post with mistakes back to the form's page, which the site then sends with Cache-Control: private, no-store (see Visitor forms).

Each server also keeps some work in memory, without a setting:

  • Markdown rendered to HTML, up to 32 MB in all; when full, the cache starts over. Text that shows media is kept per language, and for a minute at most.
  • What it read of each media file, such as its size, focal point and alt texts, for a minute.
  • sitemap.xml, for 10 seconds, or until what visitors see changes on the same server.

Changes made on the same server show at once; see The output cache. For other servers, see Several servers on one database.

The site search allows each visitor 30 searches a minute (frontend.DefaultSearchThrottle). More get the search page with status 429 Too Many Requests, without results and with SearchView.Throttled set, so the template can say why; see Search and SEO. Only searches with a query count. To change the limit, call app.Frontend.SetSearchThrottle(limit, window) after Start and before serving; a limit of zero turns it off.

The output cache

Each server keeps the pages it sends visitors in memory and sends them again without rendering them. It is on by default. Two settings of the Performance card set it:

  • The site keeps pages in memory for: 1 minute by default, or 10 seconds, 5 or 15 minutes, or Off.
  • Memory for kept pages: 32 MB by default, or 8, 64, 128 or 256 MB. When it is full, the pages not asked for the longest are dropped first.

Config.OutputCacheTTL overrides the time, and Config.Development and Config.ReloadTemplates turn the cache off unless it is set; see Configuration.

The cache keeps the answers to GET requests for pages, module pages and their feeds, sitemap.xml and robots.txt that have status 200, with their headers and their ETag, and answers GET and HEAD requests with them. It keeps a page apart for every address, query included, and for the request headers the page varies on, such as those of HTMX and Accept-Encoding. A whole page and an HTMX navigation of the same address vary on different headers, so they are kept side by side, up to four such kinds per address; beyond that, the kind stored least recently is dropped. When many visitors ask at once for a page that is not kept, it is rendered once for each kind, and the others wait for it. Cookies count for nothing, such as a site's analytics, except one a module names with Env.PersonalCookie because its pages show something per visitor by it, such as the polls module's wt_poll: the cache then keeps a page apart for each of its values. Only two kinds of cookie keep a request from the cache, those below; any other cookie of the site that changes what its pages show must be named with Env.PersonalCookie (see Caching and testing a module), or visitors get the page kept for someone else. Left out are:

  • requests with the admin's session cookie, wt_admin, so signed-in editors always get a fresh page;
  • requests with a wt_form_<key> cookie, which brings a visitor's post with mistakes back to its form (see Visitor forms);
  • previews of revisions, with ?revision=;
  • searches with a query;
  • other statuses, such as the 404 page and redirects;
  • answers that are private or no-store, that set a cookie, or whose body is over 1 MB;
  • the admin, /media/, /assets/, /theme/ and the visitor actions at /_/, which have their own caching or none.

Changes made on the same server show at once: changes to the published pages, saved site settings and theme values, changes in the media library, the publications the scheduler carries out, every post to a module's admin section or to the trash, and every visitor's post to an action at /_/ or to a page. A post answered with an error status changes nothing, and neither does a visitor's post that says it stored nothing, such as spam, a post with mistakes or one over the throttle.

Changes made from Go on the same server show at once too. The pages, the site settings and the media library count their own changes, and the bundled modules' stores tell the app once the write is committed: when an item is published, unpublished, moved to the trash or back, and when an item of a collection, such as a banner, is saved or moved. The services of the comments, polls and registrations modules tell it too. Writes of newsletter subscribers, submissions and redirects do not: no page shows subscribers or submissions, and redirects are answered before the cache. Modules tell the cache about other changes themselves; see Caching and testing a module. For other changes, such as data the site's pages show from elsewhere, the site's own code calls app.Changed() after the commit.

sitemap.xml follows the same changes, so a page published on this server is in the next sitemap at once. Changes made by another server, and what changes with time alone, such as an event that has passed, show once a kept page is older than the cache's time. In sitemap.xml, a change made by another server can take up to 10 seconds plus the cache's time.

The cache does not change what browsers and caches are told: a kept page has the same Cache-Control and ETag as a new one, and a kept feed the same Last-Modified. It answers If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since with 304 Not Modified itself, from a page it keeps that is still current. A CDN that keeps pages for Browsers and caches keep pages for may get a page from the output cache, so a change made by another server can take both times to reach visitors.

The modules' middleware, such as that of the stats and redirects modules, runs before the cache and sees every request for a page, also those the cache answers.

The metrics count the cache's hits, misses, skips and evictions and show what it holds; see Metrics and tracing. With Config.Development and OutputCacheTTL, responses say in X-Cache how the cache answered: hit, miss or skip.

The content API

With Config.API on, the site also serves its published content as JSON at /api/v1/; see Content API. Its requests pass, in this order, CORS and the rate limit, the output cache, compression and the ETag:

  • The output cache keeps the API's answers as it keeps pages, and the same changes have them made again. Searches with a query are not kept. The API reads no cookies, so the requests of signed-in editors are answered from the cache too.
  • Answers with status 200 have a weak ETag, and a client that sends it in If-None-Match gets 304 Not Modified while the answer has not changed. Their Cache-Control is that of pages, Browsers and caches keep pages for, so a CDN may keep them as long as pages. Searches with a query and errors are sent with no-cache. A single page, at /api/v1/pages/{id} or /api/v1/pages/resolve, and a module's single item, such as a post or an event, also have a Last-Modified, the latest date of what they show, and If-Modified-Since gets 304 while none of it is newer. Lists, the site and searches have none, as an item can leave a list without a newer date; see Content API.
  • Compress responses applies to the API as to pages.
  • The rate limit, 300 requests a minute per client unless Config.API.RateLimit says otherwise, comes before the output cache, so answers from the cache count too. It knows clients by their address: behind a proxy, list the proxy in TrustedProxies, or every client has the proxy's address and they share one limit. A request over the limit gets 429 with Retry-After, the window in seconds. Each server counts in its own memory, and a CDN that answers from its own cache keeps those requests from the count.
  • CORS also comes before the output cache, so an answer from the cache gets the headers for the origin of each request. With Config.API.AllowedOrigins, every answer says Vary: Origin, also one to a request without an Origin, so a CDN keeps the answers for each origin apart, and an answer without CORS headers apart from those for the allowed origins. Browsers keep the answer to a preflight request for ten minutes.
  • Like every response, the API's answers carry X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Referrer-Policy, but no framing headers; see Security headers.

The metrics and the access log count the API's requests under the route class api; see Metrics and tracing.

Health checks

Two addresses are answered before the site, its middleware and sessions, for load balancers and orchestrators:

  • /healthz answers 200 ok while the process answers requests, also before the app has started. Use it to check that the process is alive.
  • /readyz answers 200 ready when the app has started, the database answers, every schema version this start applied is still in the database, and the media storage can be reached. Otherwise it answers 503 not ready, and logs the reason as a warning. It waits at most 3 seconds. Use it to decide whether the server gets traffic.

The built-in storage checks that its folder can be read; other storage is checked when it implements media.Pinger, as contrib's s3 does by checking its bucket. Both answer GET and HEAD only; other methods go on to the site, which answers with its 404 page. Both answers are sent with Cache-Control: no-store, and neither shows up in the access log or the metrics. App.Ready(ctx) runs the same check from your own code.

In Kubernetes, with WEBTHINGS_LISTEN=:8092:

livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8092
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /readyz
    port: 8092

Metrics and tracing

App.Metrics() writes the app's metrics in the Prometheus text format:

  • webthings_http_requests_total by route class, method and status code, and webthings_http_request_duration_seconds by route class. The classes are admin, action, asset, media, seo, operations, api, for the content API, and public. The health and metrics addresses themselves are left out, so operations only counts the router's redirects to them, such as from //healthz.
  • webthings_http_requests_in_flight and webthings_start_time_seconds.
  • webthings_render_total and webthings_render_duration_seconds by render kind, for the templates of the themes, e-mail included, and the admin. An e-mail's subject and text count as kind text.
  • The database's connection pool, such as webthings_db_open_connections and webthings_db_wait_count_total, and webthings_db_statements_total.
  • The output cache: webthings_output_cache_hits_total, webthings_output_cache_misses_total, webthings_output_cache_skips_total for the GET and HEAD requests it left alone, such as editors' and the admin's, and webthings_output_cache_evictions_total for pages it dropped to stay within its memory or its four kinds per address; webthings_output_cache_entries and webthings_output_cache_bytes are what it holds now.
  • go_goroutines.

With Config.MetricsToken set, the site serves them at /metrics to requests with Authorization: Bearer <token>; other requests get 401. Without a token, /metrics answers a plain 404. Its answers are sent with Cache-Control: no-store. To keep the metrics off the public address, serve them on an address only the monitoring reaches:

if err := app.Start(ctx); err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

// The metrics on an address only the monitoring reaches.
go func() {
    internal := http.NewServeMux()
    internal.Handle("GET /metrics", app.Metrics())

    log.Println(http.ListenAndServe("127.0.0.1:9100", internal))
}()

if err := app.ListenAndServe(ctx, ":8092"); err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

Each process counts its own requests, so scrape every server. The counts leave out the health and metrics addresses. They include the answers the router gives itself, such as the redirect of //en/ to /en/.

Config.Telemetry plugs in tracing and other instrumentation. Middleware wraps the same requests as the metrics, inside the request ID and outside the access log. RenderStages run in every render of the themes and the admin, and RenderEvents receive go-partial's diagnostic events, for example go-partial's exp/otel sink. Core brings no tracing library of its own: integrations with OpenTelemetry belong in go-webthings-contrib, with the other outside dependencies.

Logs

Without Config.LogFormat, go-webthings logs with Go's default logger, slog.Default(), as the site set it up; the starter leaves it alone, so the log is text on standard error. LogFormat text or json makes the start log to standard error in that format, from LogLevel up, Info by default.

Config.AccessLog adds a line request for every request but those to the health and metrics addresses, at level Info, with these fields: method, path without the query (which may hold tokens), status, bytes as sent (after compression), duration_ms, class (as in the metrics) and request_id. Like the metrics, it includes the answers the router gives itself, such as redirects to a clean path. With LogFormat, a LogLevel above Info leaves these lines out.

Every request has an ID. A proxy may send one in X-Request-ID: it is kept when it has at most 64 letters, digits, -, _, . or :, and replaced by a new one otherwise. nginx sends its own with proxy_set_header X-Request-ID $request_id;. Every response names the ID in X-Request-ID, also before the app has started, so a visitor's report can be found in the log. With LogFormat, every line logged with a request's context carries it as request_id. Configuration shows how a logger of the site's own gets it too.

A panic in a handler is logged as panic recovered, at level Error, with the fields panic, method, path, request_id and stack. The visitor gets a plain 500, or a broken connection when the answer had already started, and the site keeps serving. The request still shows up in the access log, the metrics and Telemetry.Middleware, with its 500 or the status already sent. Before the app has started, a panic is logged the same way, with its request_id.

Development mode

Config.Development shows a failing template in detail, on the site and in the admin: the template and the line, with status 500. It also makes {{debug .}} show the value it gets. It is for your own machine only, because it shows anyone the inside of the site. The starter and the demo turn it on, with ReloadTemplates, only when WEBTHINGS_DEVELOPMENT is true, as task dev sets it, and then log development mode (WEBTHINGS_DEVELOPMENT): … at start.

Without it, a failing template, or a module's handler or visitor action that fails, is logged as render page with its details, such as the path and the module, and the visitor gets the theme's 500.gohtml with status 500, without the details: in the page's language, with the theme's partials, its asset versions and integrity, and the page's View for @model, also after a visitor action that fails. A theme without one gives go-partial's plain error page with status 500: the heading "Internal Server Error" and the message "Something went wrong. Please try again.", both translated into the page's language with the site's translations, and that language in lang. A theme's 500.gohtml gets the translated heading as .Title; see Templates. The plain page never names the failed template or the error, also when the theme's 500.gohtml or the admin's error page fails itself. See Templates. The admin answers with an error page of its own, in the admin's language and with that language in lang, and a request for part of an admin page, such as a dashboard list, with the error message "The request failed. Please try again.", both with status 500. The admin's handlers answer other unexpected errors with the same sentence: as an error message on the page for the admin's HTMX requests, as plain text for any other request. {{debug .}} then shows nothing, so a template may keep it. ReloadTemplates and Insecure are for development only as well. Development and ReloadTemplates turn the output cache off, unless Config.OutputCacheTTL is set.

The start checks every template of every theme. In development it fails with every problem it finds. Without development each problem is a warning, template problem, with the file, the line and a hint, and the start fails only for one every page of the active theme would fail with: its layout, regions or partials do not parse or call a function the site does not have, such as one of a module removed from app.Use. A template call that would show nothing, such as an instance key, an asset file or a theme setting the site does not have, is logged once as template mistake, and the page renders without it. See Checking the templates at start.

Several servers on one database

Several processes can serve one site from one PostgreSQL or MySQL database:

  • Changes made on one server show up on the others within CacheTTL, 30 seconds by default. A shorter time costs more queries; a negative one turns the cache off.
  • Changes to media, such as an alt text or a focal point, can take up to two minutes. Each server keeps what it read of a media file for a minute, and Markdown it rendered with media for a minute as well. CacheTTL does not change these times.
  • Each server keeps its own sitemap.xml for 10 seconds, so a change made on another server can take that much longer to show in it.
  • Each server has its own output cache. A page it keeps shows a change made on another server only once it is older than the cache's time, 1 minute by default, so add that time to the ones above.
  • Each server dates the feeds itself (Last-Modified; see Caching and compression), so a reader that asks with If-Modified-Since alone gets the whole feed once from every server. While a server has not seen a change made on another one yet, it may give the older feed a later time than the newer feed has there, and such a reader then keeps the older feed until the feed changes again. Readers that send the ETag are not affected.
  • Uploads must be in storage that every server reaches, such as S3. With the default storage, each server has its own media/ folder.
  • Sign-in sessions are kept in the database, so editors stay signed in on every server and after a restart.
  • The admin refuses form posts from other websites by the headers browsers send, without tokens. Any server can take any admin request, so no sticky sessions are needed, and open forms keep working after a restart.
  • Every server may run the scheduler: each planned change is made by one of them.
  • Throttles on visitors' forms and on the site search count per server, and so does the rate limit of the content API.
  • Who else is on an admin page is kept in each server's memory. Editors see each other only when their browsers reach the same server, so with several servers the header's chips can miss people.

Scheduled publishing

Editors can plan a page, post or event to be published or unpublished later. The app checks every ScheduleInterval, 30 seconds by default, and publishes with the same effects as the publish button. A negative interval stops the background scheduler; then call app.RunSchedules(ctx) from your own code.

Mail and storage

mail.SMTP is built in. It uses port 587 unless Port is set, and STARTTLS when the server offers it; port 465 with implicit TLS is not supported. Sending a message stops when its context ends or after Timeout, 30 seconds by default. See E-mail.

The E-mail step of the setup guide (see Set up the site) shows administrators how the site sends. For mail.SMTP it says "The site sends e-mail with SMTP smtp.example.com:587, from …", with the server, its port and the From address, never the username or password. Without a sender it says "No sender configured: e-mail is written to the server log, not sent." When BaseURL is empty, it warns that links in e-mail then use the address each visitor used, and that outside local development the admin offers no password reset. Send a test e-mail to … sends a short message to the signed-in administrator and waits for it, at most 30 seconds. The message afterwards says whether it went, with the sender's error when it did not; a test that went finishes the step. Each administrator may send one test e-mail every 30 seconds; another is refused with "Wait half a minute before you send another test e-mail."

A sender of your own describes itself by implementing mail.Describer, a method Describe() string, as mail.SMTP, mail.Log and mail.Memory do. Leave secrets, such as passwords and API keys, out of the description. A sender without it shows as "The site sends e-mail with the sender its code sets." See E-mail.

Uploads are kept in StateDir/media and served at /media/. Config.Storage puts them elsewhere; resized copies of images are still served at /media/, whatever the storage. See Media and images.

Integrations with outside services live in the separate repository github.com/donseba/go-webthings-contrib:

  • mailjet: Mailjet as the mail sender, and a list sync for the newsletter module.
  • s3: media storage on S3-compatible stores, such as AWS S3, DigitalOcean Spaces and MinIO.

Shutting down

The starter cancels its context on SIGINT and SIGTERM. ListenAndServe (or Serve) then stops accepting connections, gives running requests up to 5 seconds, and closes the app: it stops the scheduler and the cleanup of expired sessions, lets modules finish for up to 10 seconds, and closes the storage and the database. Modules write what they keep in memory, such as page views and redirect hits; a newsletter mailing stops after the current message and continues at the next start. Closing the app also ends the admin's open event streams.

Give the process about 15 seconds after SIGTERM before it is killed.

Sitemap and robots.txt

/sitemap.xml lists every published page in every language, with links to the other languages, and the pages that modules add below their page, such as news posts. A module whose list fails is left out and logged. The sitemap holds at most 50,000 addresses, the most a sitemap file may have; beyond that, the last ones are left out and a warning is logged. Each server builds it again at once when what visitors see changes on that server, and otherwise at most once every 10 seconds, and keeps it in its output cache like a page.

/robots.txt allows every crawler everywhere and points to the sitemap. It does not name the admin, so a path of your own is not published there. Admin pages answer with X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow instead. Both use BaseURL, or the request's address without it. See Search and SEO.

Running with systemd

[Unit]
Description=example.com
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=website
WorkingDirectory=/srv/website
ExecStart=/srv/website/bin/website
StateDirectory=website
Environment=WEBTHINGS_STATE_DIR=/var/lib/website
EnvironmentFile=/etc/website.env
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

StateDirectory creates /var/lib/website for the website user. /etc/website.env holds the secrets, such as WEBTHINGS_DB_DSN and the mail password, and should be readable by root only. systemd stops the service with SIGTERM.

sudo systemctl enable --now website
journalctl -u website -f

The log goes to standard error: the address it serves on, the setup link while no account exists (again at level WARN when the sign-in page is opened, at most once a minute), templates that are still missing, template problems and mistakes, a warning when BaseURL is empty, and errors. Logs describes the format and the access log.

In a container

A container image needs the same pieces:

  • a build stage with Go that builds as task build does, with CGO_ENABLED=0 and -tags nodynamic, so the runtime image can be Alpine or scratch as well as Debian slim;
  • until go-webthings has a release, its checkout in the build context, because the starter's go.mod points to ../go-webthings;
  • the binary, templates/ and translations/ in the working directory;
  • a volume for the state folder;
  • CA certificates, and time zone data unless the binary embeds it;
  • WEBTHINGS_LISTEN=:8092, so the site is reachable from outside the container;
  • a stop timeout of about 15 seconds.

Guides.Title: Using modules
Guides.Summary: Modules add content and features to the site, such as news, an agenda, comments or a newsletter. You choose them in main.go, each as one or more named instances.
Guides.Body:
Add instances

app.Use adds module instances before the app starts:

err = app.Use(
    publishing.Module("news", "News"),
    publishing.Module("blog", "Blog"),
    events.Module("agenda", "Agenda"),
    comments.Module("remarks", "Comments"),
)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

The first argument is the instance key, the second the title editors see in the admin navigation and the page editor. The key:

  • starts with a lowercase letter, followed by lowercase letters, digits and dashes, at most 64 characters in all;
  • is unique on the site;
  • is not a name core uses itself: pages, media, site, theme, mail, partials or webthings, the folder of core's own templates, nor one of the admin's own sections and pages: accounts, groups, account, assets, login, logout, setup, forgot-password, reset-password, trash or presence;
  • differs from the admin sections that other instances name after their key. Publishing news also adds the section news-categories, so another instance with that key stops app.Start with admin section "news-categories" exists twice. Directory adds <key>-categories too, and Newsletter <key>-texts.

An invalid or repeated key stops the app with an error.

The key is the instance's name everywhere: in the admin (/admin/news with the default admin path), in the addresses visitors' forms post to (/_/remarks/...) and the names of those routes (remarks.post), in template folders (news/post.gohtml) and as the first argument of template functions ({{range posts "news" 3}}). It is also stored with the instance's content, its page and the groups' permissions. A renamed key starts as an empty instance; the content of the old key stays in the database until you use that key again.

The admin navigation

Group lists an instance's admin sections under a heading in the admin's navigation, including the sections it adds next to its main one, such as news-categories:

err = app.Use(
    publishing.Module("news", "News").Group("Website"),
    events.Module("agenda", "Agenda").Group("Agenda"),
    comments.Module("remarks", "Comments").Group("Visitors"),
)

Instances without a group are listed under Modules. The admin translates the group names Agenda, Content, Visitors, Website, Communication and Shop; other names are shown as written.

The navigation starts with Dashboard, Pages and Media, then lists the groups by name, each with its sections by title, and ends with System: Accounts, Groups, Site settings, Theme, Trash and Your account. Editors can fold a group away and the browser remembers it; the group of the current section always stays open, and a folded group shows the total of its sections' counts.

Several instances of one module

Add a module as often as you need it, each time with its own key. Every instance has its own content, admin section and row in the permission matrix. Templates are found by key first, then by module type: news/post.gohtml, then publishing/post.gohtml. Instances can share one design or each have their own, and the starter's task templates -- <key> writes starting points for an instance; see Templates.

Place an instance on a page

In the admin, open a page, choose the instance under Shows on this page and publish the page. The instance then serves the page's address and everything below it: with news on the page /news, /en/news lists the posts and /en/news/<slug> shows one.

  • Only instances with public screens are offered under Shows on this page.
  • An instance is placed on one page at most, and a page with a module has no child pages.
  • An address below the page that the instance has no screen for, or a request with another method, gets the site's 404 page.
  • The instance is shown in every language the page is published in.
  • A page whose instance was removed from main.go answers with an error until it is unpublished or gets another module.

{{moduleURL "news"}} is the address of that page in the current language, or empty when the instance is on no page. Many modules also work without a page of their own, through their template functions. Their items are then still listed, but without links to pages that do not exist: .URL of {{range posts "news" 3}} is empty. The site search finds an instance's content only while it is on a page. Pages explains the page tree.

Publishing and Events also serve Atom and RSS feeds below their page: with news on /news, /en/news/feed.atom and /en/news/feed.rss list the newest posts and /en/news/category/<slug>/feed.atom and .rss those of a category; with agenda on /agenda, /en/agenda/feed.atom and .rss list the upcoming and running events. Core's head tags link to the feeds of the page shown with {{feedLinks}}, so browsers and feed readers find them; see Themes. Feeds list at most 20 items unless Items in feeds in Site settings › General says otherwise. The modules' READMEs describe the entries, and Feeds for modules explains how a module of your own offers feeds.

The pages of some modules describe their content to search engines as structured data, schema.org items in JSON-LD, which core's head tags write in the page's <head> with {{structuredData}}; see Search and SEO. Core describes the site, its organisation and the page itself; these modules add their content:

Module Structured data
Publishing A post's page is an Article, by the site's organisation.
Events An event's page is an Event, with its place and its start and end in the event's timezone.
Registrations Gives the Event of a linked events instance (ForEvents) an Offer while visitors can register or every place is taken.
People A person's page is a Person who works for the site's organisation.
Directory An entry's page is a LocalBusiness when it has opening hours, a Place when it has an address or a position, and an Organization otherwise.

The list pages of Publishing, Events, Gallery, People and Directory, and a directory category's page, add an ItemList of the item pages they show, in their order. The other bundled modules add none; their pages have core's items only. Structured data for modules explains how a module of your own adds items.

The content API

While Config.API turns on the content API, Publishing, Events, Gallery, Lists, People, Testimonials, Directory and Documents also serve their published content as JSON below /api/v1/<key>/: with news, /api/v1/news/posts lists the posts and /api/v1/news/categories the categories, and with agenda, /api/v1/agenda/events lists the upcoming and running events. Content API lists the endpoints of each, and the modules' READMEs describe their fields. An instance has its endpoints also while it is on no page; their url fields are then null. Registrations, Submissions, Forms, Comments, Polls, Newsletter, Banners, Redirects and Stats have none, so the API shows no data of visitors, such as sign-ups, form entries or subscribers. /api/v1/site lists the instances with endpoints, and The content API for modules explains how a module of your own adds some.

Options and site features

Some modules take options after the title, or a third argument:

err = app.Use(
    registrations.Module("signup", "Sign-ups", registrations.ForEvents("agenda"), registrations.Currency("GBP")),
    newsletter.Module("letters", "Newsletter", newsletter.WithProvider(provider)),
    submissions.Module("tips", "Tips", "news"),
)

Redirects and Stats are site features: one instance serves the whole site, so their key is optional. Without options they are named redirects and stats, titled "Redirects" and "Statistics". Named chooses another key and title:

err = app.Use(
    redirects.Module(),
    stats.Module(stats.Named("visits", "Visits")),
)

The stats key is then the first argument of its template functions: {{pageViews "visits" ""}}.

Bundled modules

Each module is documented in its README, also published at https://modules.gowebthings.com.

Module Add with What it does
Publishing publishing.Module(key, title) News and blogs: dated posts with categories, drafts, scheduled publishing and feeds
Events events.Module(key, title) An agenda of events with dates, a location, drafts, scheduled publishing and a feed
Gallery gallery.Module(key, title) Photo albums with images from the media library
Lists lists.Module(key, title) Short ordered lists, such as an FAQ or services
Testimonials testimonials.Module(key, title) Quotes from customers or partners
People people.Module(key, title) Staff, team or board, with a page per person
Documents documents.Module(key, title) Downloads by category and year, with a counter
Directory directory.Module(key, title) Organisations and places with opening hours, search and CSV import
Banners banners.Module(key, title) Hero slides and announcement bars, with an optional time window
Forms forms.Module(key, title) A form built in the admin, with an inbox and notification mail
Polls polls.Module(key, title) Questions with options and one vote per visitor
Comments comments.Module(key, title) Comments below any content, and guestbooks, with moderation
Registrations registrations.Module(key, title, options...) Sign-ups for events or other subjects, with places, prices and confirmation mail
Submissions submissions.Module(key, title, target) Visitors propose news; editors accept it as a draft post
Newsletter newsletter.Module(key, title, options...) Double opt-in signup and mailings
Redirects redirects.Module(options...) Old addresses to new ones, with hits and missed paths
Stats stats.Module(options...) Page views without cookies, and "most read" lists

Template functions and components

Modules add template functions that every template can use, with the instance key as first argument. Functions that return content give it in the page's language:

{{range posts "news" 3}}<a href="{{.URL}}">{{.Title}}</a>{{end}}
{{range entries "faq"}}<h3>{{.Title}}</h3>{{.Body}}{{end}}

Images come as <X>URL, a WebP copy at most 1600 pixels wide, never the uploaded original, with <X>Srcset, <X>Width and <X>Height for the img tag and <X>OriginalURL for downloads, such as a post's ImageURL or a person's PhotoURL:

{{range posts "news" 3}}{{if .ImageURL}}<img src="{{.ImageURL}}" srcset="{{.ImageSrcset}}" sizes="100vw" width="{{.ImageWidth}}" height="{{.ImageHeight}}" alt="">{{end}}{{end}}

Media and images explains the copies and the image and srcset functions for other sizes.

Components are template functions that render a whole part of a page with default markup, such as a comment thread with its form:

{{commentThread "remarks" .ID}}
{{pollBox "survey" ""}}
{{newsletterForm "letters"}}

A theme replaces a component's markup with <key>/<name>.gohtml or <type>/<name>.gohtml, for example remarks/thread.gohtml. Template functions covers the functions core adds, and Visitor forms the forms components contain.

Module Functions Components
Publishing posts
Events events
Gallery albums, album
Lists entries
Testimonials testimonials
People people, peopleIn, person
Documents documents, documentsIn
Directory directoryEntries, directoryEntry, directoryCategories
Banners banners, banner
Polls polls, poll, pollURL pollBox
Comments comments, commentCount, commentURL, commentInput, commentResult, commentsClosed commentThread, commentForm
Registrations registration, registerURL, registrationResult, registrationCode registrationForm
Submissions submitURL, submitInput, submitResult
Newsletter newsletter, newsletterURL, newsletterResult newsletterForm
Stats pageViews, popular

Forms and Redirects have no template functions. Each module's README describes its functions.

Comments, Newsletter, Polls, Registrations and Submissions also hand templates their visitor forms as .Form (Comments through commentInput and Submissions through submitInput too), so a template that lays out a form itself renders it with go-form's functions. form_open writes the form tag with the spam trap and the page to return to: the element whose id is the instance key, or a poll's .Anchor. form_field renders a field by the key of its name tag, with its label and limits, and the fields' ids start with the instance key, such as letters-email:

{{with newsletter "letters"}}
    <div id="letters">
        {{form_open .Form}}
            {{form_field .Form "locale" nil}}
            {{form_field .Form "email" nil}}
            <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
        {{form_close}}
    </div>
{{end}}
